If this had not happened to him, we would have had an arsenal of notes on his exposition of the Psalms, as we see in the review he made of other treatises. From the beginning of his conversion we see the Saint, in the villa of Casiciaco, immersed in the reading and meditation of the Psalms, because although he suggested to Saint Ambrose that he tell him what he should read in that retreat from the Holy Scripture to prepare and prepare to receive baptism, not having understood the reading of the prophet Isaiah that he ordered, he left it for when he was more exercised and adapted to the divine language, as he tells us in his Confessions. On the contrary, the reading and meditation of the Psalms captivated his spirit, in such a way that he would have liked the whole world to recite them with him so that it would be ignited with love for God, since he noticed in his spirit the light that the divine mysteries gave off, the affections of hope and joy, fear and horror, mercy, humility and greatness that they instilled in his heart, being abundant food to repair the weakness and weakness of the human heart. However, perhaps he would never have decided to expound the entire Psalter if for a set of reasons he had not been forced to do so. In addition to the abundant moral and theological doctrine that the Psalms contain, with which perfect Christians could be formed, the circumstance was that at that time the Psalter, with the Gospel and the Epistles of the Apostles, was the most read books of Scripture, and it can be said that they were in

hands of all the faithful; Well then it was instituted, as Augustine himself stated, that the Psalms be sung, according to the Eastern custom, in the churches of the West, the church of Milan being one of the first to establish this custom. Knowing, therefore, the faithful of the material meaning of the Psalms, it was necessary that they not only know the letter, because the letter kills and the spirit gives life. As this spiritual knowledge of the Psalms was not available to everyone, and even the material meaning itself contained many obscurities, the same faithful, eager for their perfect Christian formation, urged the Saint to expound the Psalms, as we can see in many of his expositions, and mainly in the prologue that Saint Augustine himself inserted to Psalm 118 and in letter 169 (n. l), to Evodio, where he says: "They earnestly ask me let him expound the psalms that I have not yet treated. Therefore, as, on the one hand, he saw the arsenal of doctrine contained in the Psalms, and, on the other, the superficial knowledge that the faithful had of them, and their continuous requests and requests, and, above all, the obligation he had as a shepherd to shepherd his flock, he determined to complete the exposition after much work, with such ardor that "I do not want," he says, "to be diverted or delayed from this by any other questions that come my way." From the same reading of his exposition to the Psalms we see that he did not have a rigorous order in it, but rather he adapted to the time, the circumstances, the people who demanded it of him. Nor did he expound all the Psalms in homiletic form: some he preached, others he wrote and gave them to the people, and others, while preaching them, copied them to them. In the preaching of the Psalms he used to read some similar passage from the Gospel or the Epistles of the Apostles, to which he refers very frequently in the body of the exposition of the psalm. With time he had given precise norms for the interpretation of all Holy Scripture in his books De Doctrina christiana. For the same reason, he now adjusts to them in the exposition of the Psalms. At all times he was a staunch defender of the literal meaning of Scripture; Thus, he now tries above all to clarify this meaning, taking the Latin editions as a basis for his work.

When he observes any discrepancy in them, he resorts to the Greek codices, and through them he often corrects the translation variants that he observes in the Latin ones; for thus he writes in the epistle to Audacius: «I have not translated, but rather I have corrected the errors of the Latin codices, using the Greek codices. Of this

So perhaps I made a more appropriate reading, although perhaps not the appropriate one. But since the literal sense says very little to the spirit, and taking into account that the letter kills and the spirit gives life, and that God gave his writings for the spiritual benefit of men, and that the Apostle says that all the things that took place in the Old Testament happened in figures and were written for our teaching, after clarifying the literal meaning he exposes the spiritual or figurative meaning, thus elevating the hearts of his faithful from earth to heaven. The reading of the Psalms so captured his spirit throughout his life that he said goodbye to the world by reciting them. FR. BALBINO MARTÍN PÉREZ, O. S. A.

The impression made on Augustine by his first contact with the Psalms would insinuate into his heart, always open to reflection and feeling, the most vivid expressions of the spiritual. When he tells us about his elevations in the melodies heard in the basilica of Milan and when he later reminds us of the evisceration of Davidic feelings in his soul, in Casiciaco, he is evoking the sweetness of his father's house, eager to surrender to the divine, bored by the traffic of the world and made a heavy burden for himself. The account of the Confessions in this regard is significant: Quantum flevi in ​​hymnis et canticis tuis suavi sonantis ecclesiae tuae vocibus commotus acriter! If Augustine's spirit continually lived on great psychological emotions, it is true that the truth entered his ear with the sweet melody of the Church. In a simple confession—he was already a bishop—he remembers the delights of hearing and the dangers of it, but admits the truth, the means of apostolate that music with good feelings means. With a certain exaggeration of a saint he examines the pleasures of hearing and reproaches himself that sometimes he gives in to his taste, but then he emerges and rises bravely to a higher region. So much so, that he has been tempted to discard the custom of singing the Psalms in church or to do it like Athanasius of Alexandria, who ordered it to be sung with a voice so soft that it seemed more like a reading than a song 5. But the experience and the step that tears in contact with sacred music represent for his conversion did not allow him to achieve the conceived purpose: «However, when I remember the tears that I shed with the songs of the Church at the beginning of my conversion and what moves me now, not with singing, but with the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and a very convenient modulation, I recognize once again the great usefulness of this custom. Thus I fluctuate between the danger of delight and the experience of profit, although I am more inclined—without giving an irrevocable ruling in this—to approve the custom of singing in church, so that the weak spirit may be awakened to piety by the delight of the ear. However, when I feel moved more by singing than by what is sung, I confess that I sin in it and deserve punishment, and then I would like more not to hear singing. The beginning is already announced by the Saint. Personal experience has not allowed him to go against a healthy custom. At least those who are incapable of elevating themselves in any other way to the feelings of adhesion and love to the Almighty should do so through the Psalms. Saint Augustine, then, does not reject the custom of singing the Psalms in church and faces the dangers it can offer. He personally confesses his fault, when there is one, and warns the faithful about the same. The experiential experience of the Saint allows him to give a judgment on the issue debated in various environments. He is not opposed, but he wants to instruct: here is his program.

If the faithful are to listen to the Psalms and other songs daily in the church, and the essential thing about the song is not the sound, but what is said, what is meant in the words, that is, the feelings that it conveys.

He has already posed the pastoral problem of music and singing in the Christian life and solves it wonderfully with immense work, in meditation and solitude, communicated and spoken out loud. The usefulness of his neighbor is the norm of his apostolic life, and he dedicates himself to it with greater love the greater the benefit he foresees to follow. Thus he can write to Evodio, regarding the Enarrationes, that "he has dictated the exposition of three new psalms, 67, 71 and 77, at considerable length. Everyone expects and demands hard from me what I have not yet taught or studied. I don't want to be taken away from this and delayed in any other issues that come my way. I don't even want to continue now the books On the Trinity, which I have had in my hands for a long time and which I have not yet finished. They make me too tired, and I imagine that there are few who will understand them; I am most urgent about those that, according to my hope, will be useful to many. The key is given. It will not be, therefore, a masterful theological work, with great exegetical or philosophical disquisitions, but rather a personal, experiential, experiential work, for the benefit of the public. It will be a work of adapting the great truths of Christianity to an ordinary public that seeks to take advantage of the teachings that it continually hears in church singing, and that enters its ear almost without perceiving the greatness of the message. Saint Augustine does not write or dictate the Enarrationes with the desire of a scientist, but with a desire for profit. We will see it in each of its pages. This does not prevent them from touching on all theological and biblical, moral and spiritual issues, plainly, so that the faithful understand it and are not scandalized by anything. The demands of Christianity are expressed clearly and forcefully, as a sweet burden of love, not as an authoritarian imposition. St. Augustine's Expositions of the Psalms would thus be like the modern "commentator's book," a guide to the understanding of the Psalms. Gorla writes that “these Augustinian commentaries are the psalms of the Psalms. The thought returns: Augustine is the true David of the New Testament" 8.

We will see the general Augustinian method immediately, but the questions that this great work poses to the informed reader are very varied. In this section we will limit ourselves to the following, which we will deal with as briefly as possible, since we do not intend to resolve the controversies, but rather to warn the reader of their existence: a) place where they were preached; b) auditorium; c) chronology. In advance, however, we must note that not all the Expositions of the Psalms were preached. We have already seen that in Epistle 169, to Evodio, he spoke of dictati et tractati, although we do not know the precise meaning of the two terms. It is true, however, according to the authors and judging, above all, from the Enarratio in psalmum 118, that some were preached to the people and others dictated, undoubtedly, before the stenographers: Psalmos omnes caeteros, quos codicem Psalmorum novimus continere, quod Ecclesiae consuetudine Salterium nuncupatur, partim sermocinando in populis, partim dictando exposui, Domino donor, sicut potuiln. And now he will expound Psalm 118 by writing it in the form of homilies, so that it can be preached to the people. Consequently, the great majority of the Expositions were preached to the people, and others have been dictated before the stenographers. These sermons, however, to Psalm 118 have been written in the form of homilies, to be preached to the people, as other Holy Fathers of the Church did, especially Saint Ambrose and Saint John Chrysostom."

It depends on this that we can precisely define the audience of the Enarrationes and that we can see Saint Augustine in the various environments to which he had to present himself, and to which he had to adapt his vision and his ordinary way of preaching. In fact, until the present it had been believed that Carthage had been the place where Augustine gave his Expositions of the Psalms to the public. The arguments in favor were sought in the literary style, in the images, in the most elevated concepts and in the most refined and strictly rhetorical prose. General introduction

It would be easy, since we would have to assume, something almost certain today, that Augustine, during the time that Valerius allowed him to prepare himself in Scripture before his consecration, would collect certain exegesis cards that would serve him for sermons and expositions of Scripture. This appears clearly in the first enarrations, where he still adheres quite closely to the traditional, to the exposition that other ancient authors have made, especially up to the Enarratio in ps. 31. The argument of the monks, who appear almost continuously in the gradual psalms, would not serve for Le Landais, since monasteries of Augustinian influence, direct or indirect, existed not only in Carthage, but also in Hippo, in Tagaste and in many other places. However, we believe that the sermons, as presented especially in En. in ps. 132 and in 99, they would come much better in Carthage, where the disturbances would be found, and which Augustine warned about. This does not prevent the fact that there were also them in Hippo even then, as they appeared later, when Augustine had to address the people to expose the life of his monks and cleanse them of the evil tongues of the faithful. The argument would conclude and stand. Nor would the argument of the theater or the circus work, because, although it is true that the metropolis abounded in all of this, we already know, from the discoveries and excavations of Hippo, that all of this occurred in North Africa, and even in Tagaste, apparently, Romaniano himself exhibited certain theater or circus games. Summarizing, then, this first point about the place of preaching of the sermons on the Psalms of Augustine, we will say that a great majority, according to the authors, have been delivered in Carthage; others, the enarrations to the gradual psalms, according to Morceaux, Willmart, De Bruyne, Zarb and Pontet, were also in the African capital and, according to Le Landais, in Hippo; and others, as we have seen, In ps. 34 in Tagaste and In ps. 144 in Utica. The efforts that are being carried out to decide with greater precision the place of each of them will see happy success and we hope for their prompt appearance. We do not even attempt—it would be impossible for us—to define the precise church or basilica in which they were preached. In some we would have the name given in certain passages, but it is uncertain for the vast majority, and it interests us less for the purpose we pursue.
Carthage, then, or Hippo, without discounting other towns in North Africa, have been the theater of Augustine's desire for perfection.

The mere fact of presenting ourselves as a theater of the Augustinian word Carthage represents for us the image of a mixed audience, of the most diverse quality and made for the most varied emotions and expressions. Augustine, when adapting to the public, would, in fact, have to take into account the diversity of psychology and adapt its expression to the various types that appear in that world. From the sailors and porters of the port to the high-born intellectuals, who would approach the chair of Agustín, whose memory as a schoolboy and a rhetorician endured in the great city, would hear the comments. An audience, then, of the most compact guarantee and of the maximum difficulty for the preacher. Agustín did not fear the public, because he knew how to gain trust and knew how to attract the attention of his listeners. It is not surprising, then, that in these sermons annotations of all kinds appear, psychological images that touch all social groups, banners that stick into all the loins of society, touches to the heart and attacks to the intelligence. As in Rome, the capital of the world, Carthage, emulating it in every way, was mixed in a hybrid mass of grammarians and mathematicians, heretics of all kinds and types with pagans or those without divinity. From the bardings that he tells us about in the City of God to the virgins and monks that appear in other exhibitions, there is not a state of life that does not find its own place in these Enarrationes. Saint Augustine enjoys the flexibility of spirit necessary to make applications to all states of life, to all Christians, and to place himself in the psychological emotion of the individual to whom he wants to adapt his message 23. There are, therefore, in his audience the drunks, the impure, the greedy, the men eager for solitude who seek to withdraw from the tumult of the public to live peacefully in solitude and retirement, and there they follow themselves. Here we will find precisely the key to the underlying problems debated in the Enarrationes. There is, however, something more, something that perhaps is less obvious in this Augustinian work than in any other. Heresies and schisms: the Donatists, attacking the unity of the Church; The Pelagians, the Arians on occasion, and not infrequently the Manichaeans, appear interspersed in the present work.

In them, therefore, a deranged world will be exhibited, a world that groans or a world that cries, a world that seeks a way out of its problems and will only find it in Christ. For this reason, Augustine's present audience is the Carthaginian, or perhaps that of Hippo on occasions; but in its audience, in its men of vice or in its men of virtue, it has posed the problem of the world, it rises to world class, and hence the basic relevance of these immortal exhibitions. In all of Augustine's works there are underlying themes that are repeated and are not studied because they are so abundant. In the Enarrationes we will now try a synthesis of the biblical exegesis of the Psalms and its problems, and some brief reflections on Christ and the Church.

Augustine's novelty in his Enarrationes is not reduced to exposition, nor even to exegesis. Many other Fathers had tried, totally or partially, to comment on the Psalter. Saint Augustine, as has also happened with the Gospel of Saint John, entered into the Psalms with a desire for perfection, as he directed all his biblical expositions towards it, and, consequently, he was going to dispense a little with the technique, with the rules given for exegesis in the De doctrina christiana, and would involve himself in the problems of life and practical applications. This does not prevent him from resorting very frequently in his comments, in this one more than in any other work, to Greek, to philology, we would say, and searching through the word for the spiritual meaning that he intends to give to the text. Augustinian exegesis, which is not a philological technique, is a profound meditation on the abundant themes that summarize Scripture in short sentences. We do not go into elucidating the question of the multiplicity of literal meanings or not, nor the various spiritual or mystical meanings that Augustine 2 can admit. We are interested in stating that Augustine cannot be asked, as it would be unfair to ask any Father of the Church, for an exegesis based on comparative philology and extra-biblical texts, as a scripturist of our days can do. Saint Augustine follows the molds of the exegesis of his time, and more specifically the double influence he suffered in his written training.

With this first principle of Christological spirituality, it is not surprising that the basis of the great Augustinian work is precisely perfection as a common enterprise of all men, not only of an elite or of some not so qualified. Admire the insistence with which Augustine resorts to becoming aware of belonging to Christ, of being members of his mystical Body, which consequently imposes a series of acceptances of love. The perfection demanded by the Saint in his expositions is not limited; It is current and in the middle of the century in which we live. Augustine does not propose retreats or great mortifications; It only tries to Christianize all environments, to give the faithful the awareness that they can be perfect in any state of life in which they participate. Being members of that Christ who wanted us to gather everyone in himself, redeeming ourselves, we all have to see Christ in our brothers and see Christ in each of our actions. All classes of society parade throughout the Enarrationes, from the slave and the drunk to the bishop, nuns and virgins. The multiple experiences lived by the Saint enabled him to understand the various states in which the will of God can be followed. Its pages are wonderful, as you can savor, in which it clearly raises the problems of married life, or of youthful life, or of shows, or of clerics, or of monastic life in its various aspects. There was no darkness in Augustine's mind, and there were only two fundamental themes that he was interested in instilling in his faithful: the possibility of being perfect in one's own state, belonging to Christ, and the acceptance of the will of God, also manifested in Christ, and which is clear in the Holy Scripture. Perfection, a common undertaking, only means that anyone can reach perfection and that everyone has to fill a measure before God. Perfection is not imposed, it must be accepted out of love, and no one is excluded from effort and work. Grace will crown one's own work, initiating it before and concurring and collaborating with the will; But it is necessary to know how to dance very well with grace so as not to step on it or be stepped on by it. In this seized dance, Saint Augustine has been an expert teacher and has played with beauty to throw the Pelagians off the dance floor, who were profaning the sacred dance of freedom and grace.

Saint Augustine could not despise the objections that he had heard countless times from his faithful and from those who for one reason or another approached him, especially in those situations in which Rome felt itself sinking under the overwhelming edge of the barbarians. As in De civitate Dei he tried in many passages to console the women who had suffered the desecration of the mob in their bodies and sought the tranquility of consciences in the face of the horrors committed by the barbarians, urging the providence that allows evils and evil to amend and increase the perfection of the good, so it happens here when he tries to solve the dilemma and put an end to that drama that continues in continuous unrest. Saint Augustine requires, above all, faith 23. Without faith there is no solution to this drama, because it is natural that those who do not believe cannot sacrifice themselves, nor love, nor give themselves out of pure humanitarianism or philanthropy. Whoever does not believe has to rebel against the evils that exist in the world and, therefore, against that God who allows them and who harasses consciences in such a way that he does not allow rest. The reflection on the good - he now addresses them -, since they are the ones who suffer the attacks, is always the same: the punishment of the bad must be an admonition, a warning and an example for the good, so as not to decline from their path 24. However, the conscience of these will still disturb the misfortunes that have happened to some of their same moral condition, and Augustine will reply to them that perhaps they too have had something to repent before God and have the opportunity to prove in that way his humility. It is necessary to begin with the fear of God 2S. To that Christian who, shaken by these objections of great shipwrecks, doubts his faith and the collected and withdrawn life he leads, the Saint reminds him that it is necessary to fear God, to begin with that servile love for those eternal punishments that exist, even if at times he has doubts against them, and from that servile fear to move on to chaste fear, which will lead him to love 26. Between fear and hope lies the game. There is, however, no true fear, no true hope, no true love without faith. Without the foundation of this faith there can be no solution nor will the drama find an outcome. Tying oneself to the cross of Christ, meditating on his tribulations and hardships, taking the resurrection as a banner to ensure the prize of the future life, will be the only way out of this alley in which humanity has imprisoned itself.

Man's attitude towards the goods of the earth is precisely indifference. What does this mean? Saint Augustine responds clearly, putting fixed points where he needs them: Nec extolli quando res prosperae accidunt, nec frangi quando res adversae sunt, sed ubique Dominum benedicere r°. Here is the precise meaning: it is not about despising material goods or rejecting them; It is not about separating yourself from the world and thinking that a retired life is easier for the service of God. The only thing to be careful is not to become conceited by prosperity nor to become broken and exhausted by adversity, but, in both cases, to know how to preserve the presence of mind and consciousness of God and bless Him. This is the Christian position towards events and towards all things. When we feel indifference we usually mean carefree. And it's not true. Spiritually, indifference to earthly goods does not translate into carelessness or disinterest in them. No. The Christian does not renounce progress, he does not renounce the values ​​of the earth; he renounces enjoying them and considering them as an end in themselves. He is called to give glory to God through the realization and putting into practice all the values ​​that God has hidden in things and to collaborate in the progress of humanity in every way. To label the Christian as retrograde because of this indifference is to not have understood the authentic, the only true meaning of relativity, which is only such in relation to the absolute and eternal. Indifference, therefore, to material happiness or prosperity is not limited to enjoying it, but tends to increase it, but it gives prosperity as well as adversity. He lives better with prosperity, but adversity does not take him away from his happiness, because he is anchored in God, he has an immobile center in his soul and no one or anything else bothers him. That is the significance that Augustine has indicated to indifference. If we transfer the issue of indifference to the psychological, we must confess that it is not a destruction of feeling or annihilation of sensitivity.

Saint Augustine knew better than anyone the profound meaning of sensitivity in life, and he wonderfully analyzes the wound caused by misunderstandings and ingratitude. Indifference does not mean not feeling, but rather, feeling,

see the hand of God in it and not get discouraged. Whoever thinks that being indifferent to what is earthly, human or cosmic is not feeling, is reaching a stoic ataraxia, goes outside the channel of Christianity; even more so, from the channel of authentic Augustinianism. Sensitivity must be nourished, it must be sheltered, it must be felt deeply to be able to appreciate the hard hand of God. When Saint Augustine spoke of the sensus doloris, he was saying that he who has lost it cannot rise to God. Sensitivity is the price of intimacy with God and leads us directly to Him along unexpected paths, but real and vital, fully existential. However, this very healthy doctrine of Augustine is also established in the group that we examine here. Indifference is not a flower of a day, it is not born by spontaneous generation. Indifference to the earthly springs from the hope of the heavenly, and this cannot exist if the desire for the homeland and the nostalgia for eternity, hope and love have not first been born in the heart. The night of the world, its darkness, must be illuminated by Christ. When Christ takes the soul by his hand and illuminates it with his wisdom, he begins to treat the things of earth indifferently. In this appendix we do not intend to make an exhaustive study of the data on monastic life that can be found in the Enarrationes in Psalmos. We simply want to frame monasticism, as Augustine conceived it, within the general margin of that perfection, which was the common enterprise of every Christian and to which the monks committed themselves in a special way. Among the public to whom the Enarrationes are addressed we sometimes find monks, explicitly or implicitly indicated. And the way the argument is treated cannot be separated from that universalized perfection for all members of the Body of Christ. We already know—and we do not want to enter into discussion here, nor even collect the bibliography, we hope to do so very soon—that monastic and secular spirituality is currently being discussed in Saint Augustine. And there is a divergence of opinions. The truth is that Augustine dedicates some specific Enarrationes to dealing with monks and their problems, and in them he only establishes with greater force and vigor the foundations that we have tried to expose in the preceding pages, as obligatory for monks as well. The most decisively monastic Enarrationes are those preached around Psalms 54, 99 and 132. The realism of life had forced him to descend a little from his first idealism and to place himself next to his monks to make them understand the "first drama of monastic life", which was the same as that of general Christian life. The title is incongruous for the conclusion that will follow, since in the Enarratio in ps. 41, which concerns us in this appendix, is not about "mysticism" or "contemplation", but about Christian life brought to its complete perfection. Augustine preferred to present life without complications, according to the ordinary course of his ideas. Today we could be distracted by great disquisitions on these two terms, and perhaps we would have to conclude like Von Ivanka in the discussion of the International Augustinian Congress in Paris in 1954: "What is the mystique?" The authors have stopped to examine the En. in ps. 41, each one carrying water to his mill. We only want to point out that throughout the exhibition the ascending and double process that we have outlined is clearly represented. Here we talk about desire, hope, pilgrimage, use of the earthly, nostalgia for the homeland, sadness and joy. They are abundant themes in all Enarrationes. Psalm 41 has given you enough inspiration to summarize them all. All these thoughts are taken from the En. Soon we hope to be able to offer another work to the public. in ps. 99.11: P L 37.1277.

Augustine's exposition begins with desire, and this is not found in everyone even within the Church, but only in those who have somehow tasted the gentleness of God. That desire is not fulfilled or filled with baptism, sed fortassis si norunt ubi peregrinentur, et quo eis transeundum sit, etiam ardentius injlammantur (n. l). Desire and pilgrimage: here is the double that we have found in each of the Augustinian pages of the Psalms. It is about desiring intelligence, light, the inseparable source of life: Curre ad fontes, desidera aquarum jontes. Apud Deum est fons vitae et insiccabilis jons: in illius luz lumen inobscurabile. Lumen hoc desidera, quemdam jontem, quoddam lumen quale non norunt oculi tui; cui lumini videndo oculus interior praeparatur, cui fonti hauriendo sitis interior inardescit. Curre ad jontem, desidera jontem: sed noli ut cumque, noli ut qualecumque animal cúrrete; ut cervus curre (n.2). And since it has to run like the deer towards the fountain, it begins an analysis of paragon motives, and will say that it must resemble it, first because of its speed (ib.), and secondly, because, for the desire to grow, it has to kill the serpents of vices, as the deer does when it goes to drink water, and by killing the serpents of earthly desires, the celestial ones increase (n.3). The deer, furthermore, carry each other's burdens and help each other on the journey, and this is what must be done in the Christian life: help men so that they all progress. And it is necessary to endure in the spiritual life, on the one hand, those blinded by their lusts, and on the other, those who insult him who runs to the fountains (n.4). They were the temptations that we have seen arise before those who ardently desire and advance determinedly towards perfection. That desire turns into thirst, but a thirst that is only felt in the pilgrimage, site in peregrinatione, site in cursu, satiabor in adventu (n.5). And while I meditate and run and am on the road, the tears of bitterness for not being in the homeland and not having reached the source, the darkness of the night and the pain of dawn, will be my daily bread (n.6). In prosperity and in adversity the tears of desire and eagerness for light and intelligence flow. The pagan or one who is engrossed in his pleasures now asks the proficient about his God. This one can answer him, but "the one does not have eyes to see him, the latter advancing with desire, turning his tears into joy (ib.).

We must expect complete health from God, and for this it is necessary to persevere in love and ascend to the end in hope: perseverance ergo ut pervenias; persevere doñee venit salus (n. l l). nor security is continually disturbed: noli sperare in te, se de Deo tuo. And if you cannot wait on yourself, your attitude is one of humility, of submission to the will of God, of making yourself minimal and not attributing anything to yourself, so that God grants everything. In itself, the human spirit will encounter only confusion and tears; in the hope of God, security and joy. Feeling like a sinner, humiliating seipsum Deo, all the gifts will come to the heart, not because he deserves them or is worthy of them, but because God gives them (n.12). And finding himself in that abyss he invokes another abyss: the abyss of the preacher, thus situated, can with his word call to another abyss, the heart of his brother, so that the divine aura of desire, hope, love, and grace may open (n.13). Invoking God is calling Him into one's own intimacy, and this must be done both in prosperity and in adversity. In the time of happiness we must do like the ant: gather for the winter of tribulation and tears (n.16). Thus, the soul concentrates on itself, prays before God, remembers the delicious days of softness and its sweetness and joys (n.17), although then it asks its God: Lord, why have you taken me away from that happiness and made me return to the weight of banality due to my human condition? (n.18). As has been seen, the En. in ps. 41 is the tightest summary of the spirituality of the Enarrationes. We wanted to conclude with this point because the discussions do not lead to anything positive, and we can note the logic of Augustine in his spiritual world. The double is always the same: joy and sadness, nostalgia and hope, desire and homeland, use and indifference. And in the world, conform to the will of God and make life a continuous prayer: quidquid egeris, bene age et laudasti Deum.

ENARRATIONS ON THE PSALMS I
[THE TWO PATHS: THAT OF THE RIGHTEOUS AND THE WICKED}

1 [v. l }. Blessed is the man who is not found in the council of the wicked. This must be understood of the Lord man, that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed is the man who is not found in the council of the wicked, as the earthly man was found, who consented, breaking the precept of God, to the insinuation of the woman deceived by the serpent. And he did not stop in the path of sinners. He certainly walked the path of sinners, being born like them, but he did not stop, because the worldly attractions did not hold him back. And he did not sit in a pestilent chair, that is, he did not proudly covet the worldly kingdom. Quite accurately, pride represents the pestilent chair, because there is hardly anyone who lacks the ambition to dominate and does not desire worldly glory. Pestilence or plague is a disease that spreads too much and takes hold of everyone or almost everyone. More precisely, "pestilential chair" is understood as a pernicious doctrine, the rumor of which spreads like cancer. Next, the order of the words abiit, stetit, sedit, move away, remain and sit must be considered. Someone turns away when he turns away from God; it stops when it delights in sin; He sits when, entrenched in his pride, he cannot return, unless He delivers him who is not in the council of the wicked, nor remains in the path of sinners, nor sits in the seat of pestilence. PSALMUS

1 [v. l]. Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum: de Domino nostro Iesu Christo, hoc est nomine Dominico, accipiendum est. Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum: sicut homo terrenus qui uxori consensit deceptae a serpente, ut Dei praecepta praeteriret. Et in via peccatorum non stetit: quia \>enit quidem in via peccatorum, nascendo sicut peccatores; sed non stetit, quia eum non tenuit ¡Ilécebra saecularis. Et in cathedra pestilentiae non sedit: noluit regnum terrenum cum superbia; quae ideo cathedra pestilentiae recte intelligitur, quia non fere quisquam est qui careat amore dominandi et humanom non appetat gloriam; pestilentia est enim morbus late pervagatus, et omnes aut penis omnes involvens. Quanquam accommodatius accipiatur cathedra pestilentiae, pernicious doctrine, cuius sermo ut cancer serpit (2 Tim 2:17). Deindeconsiderdus est ordo verborum, abiit, stetit, sedit: abiit enim ille, cum recessit a Deo; stetit, eum delectatus est peccato; sedit cum in sua superbia confirmatus, rediré non potuit, nisi per eum liberatus, qui ñeque abiit in consilio impiorum, nec in via peccatorum stetit, nec in cathedra pestilentiae sedit.

2 [v. 2 }. His will remained in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night. The law, as the Apostle says, is not established for the just. It is one thing to be in the law, and another under the law; He who is in the law, works according to it; He who is under the law is compelled to act by it. Therefore that one is free and that one is a slave. One is the written law that is imposed on those who serve, and another is what is contemplated with the mind by those who have no need for letters. He will meditate day and night, this, or is understood: without interruption; or also: by day, joy, and by night, tribulation; For of joy it is said: Abraham saw my day and was glad; and of tribulation: A7In addition, even in the night my kidneys correct me. 3 { v. 3 j. And it will be like the tree that is planted next to a riverbed, that is, next to Wisdom itself, which deigned to take man for our health; in such a way that man is the tree planted on the shore of the stream of water. It can be understood this way because in another psalm it is said: The river of God is full of water. Or it can be understood: together with the Holy Spirit, of whom it is written: He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit; and also: Whoever is thirsty, let him come and drink; and that: if you knew the gift of God and who it is that asks you for water, you would collect it from him, and he would give you living water; Whoever drinks from it will never thirst, because a fountain of living water will spring up in him to eternal life. It can also be understood together with the current of waters, for the sins of the people, since in the Apocalypse the people are represented by the waters, and the current with reason 2 [v.2]. Sed in le ge Domini Fuit voluntas eius, et in lege eius meditabitur die ac nocte. lusto non est lex posita, ut dicit Apostolus (1 Tim 1,9); sed aliud est est in lege, aliud sub lege: qui est in lege, secundum legem agit; qui est sub lege, secundum legem agitur. Ule ergo liber est, iste servus. Deinde aliud est lex quae scribitur, et imponitur servienti; aliud lex quae mente conspicitur, ab eo qui non indiget litteris.

Meditabitur die ac nocte: aut sine intermissione intelligendura est; aut die in laetitia, nocte in tribulationibus; dicitur enim: Abraham dio meum vidit, et gavisus est (lo 8,56); et de tribulatione dicitur: Insuper et usque ad noctem emendaverunt me renes mei (Ps 15,7). 3 [v.3]. Et erit tanquam lignum quod plantatum est secundum decursus aquarum: id est, aut secundum ipsam Sapientiam, quae digrata est hominem suscipere ad salutem nostram; ut ipse homo sit lignum plantatum secundum decursus aquarum: potest enim et hoc intellectu accipi, quod in alio psalmo dicitur: Fluvius Dei repletus est at¡ua (Ps 64,10). Aut secundum Spiritum sanctum, secundum quem dicitur: Ipse vos baptizabit in Spiritu sancto (Mt 3,11); et illud: Qui sitit, veniat, et bibat (lo 7,37); et illud: Si scires donum Dei, et quis est qui a te aquam petit; petisses ab eo, et daret tibi aquam vivam, unde qui biberit non sitiet in aeternum; sed ejficietur in eo jons aquae sdientis in vitctm aetemam (Ib. 6,10.13.14). Aut secundum decursus aquarum, secundum

It symbolizes the fall, which corresponds to the crime. That tree, that is, our Lord, will bear fruit, that is, it will constitute the churches of the running waters, that is, of the sinful peoples, bringing them to the path and rooting them in its teaching; and he will give it in due time, namely, after having been glorified with the resurrection and the ascension into heaven. Because then, the Holy Spirit having been sent to the apostles, strengthening them in their faith and directing them to the people, he produced the fruit of the churches. And its leaf is evergreen, that is, its word will not be in vain, because all flesh is hay, and the splendor of man is like a flower of the field; The hay withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains eternally. And all the things that it does will prosper, that is, all the things that that tree produces, which, without a doubt, are leaves and fruits, that is, words and deeds. 4 [v. 4]. Not so the wicked, not so, but (they will be blown away) like dust that the wind throws on the face of the earth. By land is here understood the same stability in God, to which it is said: the Lord is the part of my inheritance; therefore my inheritance is excellent to me; and also: Endure the Lord and keep his commandments, and he will exalt him so that you may possess the land. Likewise, according to this land, it is said: Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the land. This similarity was adduced here, because, as this visible earth supports and nourishes the man in his body, so that invisible earth nourishes and supports the inner man. From whose surface he casts the wicked populorum peccata, quia et aquae populi interpretantur in Apocalypsi (Rev 17:15); et decursus non absurde intelligitur lapsus, quod pertinet ad delictum. Lignum ergo illud, id est Dominus noster, de aquis decurrentibus, id est populis peccatoribus, trahens eos in via in radices disciplinae suae, jvuctum dabil, hoc est, constituet Ecclesias; in tempore sito, id est, postquam clariíicatus est resurrectione et ascensione in caelum. Tune enim Spiritu sancto misso Apostolis, et eis in fiducia sui confirmatis et directis in populos, fructificavit Ecclesias. Et folium eius non dccidet: id est, verbum eius non erit irritum; quia omnis caro joenum, et claritas hominis ut flos foini: joenum aruit, et flos decidit, verbum anlcni Domini manet in aeternum (Is 40:6-8).

Et omnia quaecumque jecerit prosperabuntur: id est, quaecumque illud lignum attulerit; quae omnia videlicet accipienda sunt fructus et folia, id est facta et dicta. 4 [v.4]. Non sic impi, non sic: sed tanquam pulvis quem proiicit ventus a jacie terrae. Terra hic accipienda est ipsa stabilitas in Deo, secundum quam dicitur: Dominus pars haereditatis meae, etenim haereditas mea praeclara est miki (Ps 15,5.6); secundum hanc dicitur: Sustine Dominum, et observavias eius, et exaltabit te, ut possideas terram (Ps 36,34); secundum hanc dicitur: Beati mites, quia ipsi haereditate possidebunt terram (Mt 5.4). Similitudo autem hinc ducta est; Quia ut haec terra visibilis exteriorem hominem nutrit et continet, ita illa illa terra invisibilis interiorem hominem. A cuius terrae facie proiiicit ventus im-

wind, that is, pride, since it inflates. Avoiding it, he who becomes intoxicated with the abundance of the house of God and drinks from the torrent of his love, says: Let not the feet of pride come near me. Pride casts out of this land the one who said: I will set my seat in the north and I will be like the Most High. From the surface of this earth he also threw out the one who, having consented and tasted the fruit of the forbidden tree, to be like God, hid himself from the sight of God. In a special way it can be understood that this earth belongs to the inner man, from which man was thrown out by pride, in which it was written: Why are the earth and ashes proud?, since in his life he threw away his interiorities. From where the man was thrown, it is not in vain that it is said that he threw himself. 5 £v.5j. Therefore, the wicked do not arise in judgment, since they are thrown away like dust from the face of the earth. And he very well said that what the proud people desire had to be taken away from them, that is, judging. This passage is understood more clearly by the following sentence: Nor sinners in the council of the just. What was previously said is usually repeated in this way more clearly, so that the wicked are understood as sinners; so that what was previously said "in the judgment," is now expressed as saying in the council of sinners. But if the wicked are one thing and the sinners another, even though every wicked man is a sinner, although not every sinner is wicked, the wicked will not rise in judgment, that is, they will certainly rise, but not to be judged, since they are already destined for penas cerpium, id est superbia, quia inflat. Quam cavens ille quí inebriabatur ab ubertate domus Dei, et torrente voluptatis eius potabítur, dicit: Non veniat mihi pes superbiae (Ps 35,9.12). Ab hac terra proiecit superbia eum qui dixit: Ponam sedem meam ad Aquilonem, et ero similis Altiss'mio (Is 14,13,14). Ab huius terrae facie proiecit etiarn eum qui, cum consensisset et gustasset de prohibito ligno, ut esset sicut Deus, abscondit se a facie Dei (Gen 3,6.8). Hanc terram ad interiorem hominem pertinere, et inde superbia hominem proiici, máxime ¡ntelügi potest in eo quod scriptum est: Quid superbit terra et cinis? quoniam in vita sua proiecit intima sua (Eccli 10,9.10); unde enim proiectus est, non absurde se dicitur proiecisse. 5 [v.5]. Ideo non resurgunt impii in indica: ideo scilicet, quia tanquam pulvis proiiciuntur a facie terrae.

Et bene hoc eis dixit auferri quod superbi ambiunt, id est ut iudicent, ut hoc ipsum planius dictum intelligatur sequenti sententia: Ñeque peccatores in consilio iustorum. Solet enim hoc modo I repeated planius quod superius dicitur, ut peccatores intelligantur impii; et quod supra dictum est in indica, hic dictum sit in consilio iustorum. Aut certe si aliud sunt impii, aliud peccatores; ut quanquam omnis impius peccator sit, non tamen omnis peccator sit impius. Impii non resurgunt in indica: id est, resurgent quidem, sed non ut iudicentur, quia iam poenis certissimis destinad sunt; peccatores autem

very nice but sinners will not stand in the council of the righteous, that is, to judge, but rather to be judged, since it was said of them: What is the work of each one, the game will prove it; If anyone's work remains, he will receive a reward; If someone's work is burned, he will suffer detriment, but he will be saved, but just as through the game. 6 [v.6]. Because God knows the path of the righteous. As it is said that medicine knows health, but not diseases, and yet through the art of medicine evils are known, so it can be said that the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but not that of the wicked, not because the Lord is ignorant of anything even though he says to sinners: I do not know you. So it was said: The way of the wicked will perish, but God ignores the way of the wicked. In this way it was said more bluntly; so that to ignore God is to perish, and to know is to remain; so that being belongs to the knowledge of God, and non-being to ignorance, since the Lord says: I am who I am; and also: He who exists sent me. 1 [v.1.2]. Why did the nations roar and the people ponder vain things? The kings of the earth rose up and the princes gathered against the Lord and his Christ. It was said non resurgunt in consilio iustorum, id est ut iudicent, sed forte ut iudicentur, ut de his dictum sit: Vniuscuiusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit: si cuius opus manserit, mercedem accipiet: si cuius autem opus exustum fuerit, detrimentum patietur; ipse autem salvus erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem (1 Cor 3:13-15). 6 [v.6]. Quoniam novit Dominus viam iustorum. Quemadmodum dicitur, novit salutem medicine, morbos autem non novit; et tamen etiam morbi arte farmaciae agnoscuntur; sic dici potest, nosse Dominurn viam iustorum, viam vero impiorum non nosse; non quia aliquid Dominus nescit, et tamen dicit peccatoribus: Non novi vos (Mt 7,23). Iter autem impiorum peribit, pro eo positum est, ac si diceretur: Iter autem impiorum non novit Dominus. Sed planius dictum est, ut hoc sit nesciri a Domino, quod est perire, et hoc sit sciri a Domino, quod est manere: ut ad scientiam Dei esse pertineat, ad ignorantiam vero non esse; quia Dominus dicit: Ego sum qui sum; et: Qui est, misit me (Ex 3,14). 1 [v.1.2]. Utquid frtmuerunt gentes, et populi meditati sunt inania? Asiiterunt reges terrae, et principes convenerunt in unum, adversus Domi-

why instead of in vain, because they did not carry out what they intended, that is, to put an end to Christ. Although it may be understood in another way, it is nevertheless more properly applied to the person of those who were said to have meditated on vain things; so that the meaning of breaking his chains and throwing off his yoke from us is: let us act in such a way that the Christian religion is not tied to us or imposed on us. £3 v. 4 }. He who dwells in heaven will mock them, and the Lord will mock them. As we see, the sentence is repeated, since, instead of him who lives in heaven, the Lord was then said; and instead of will mock, it was written will wet. Let nothing of this be taken carnally, as if God mocked with gestures of the mouth or scoffed with the grimaces of the nose, but rather it must be taken for that virtue which he gives to his saints, by which, seeing things to come, that is, that the name of Christ and his dominion is to be extended and established in the future and in all nations, they understand that they think vain things. This virtue by which these things are foreknown is the ridicule and mockery of God. He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them. If by heaven we understand holy souls, by them, knowing what will happen, God will mock and mock them. num, et adversas Christum eius. Pro eo dictum est utquid, ac si diceretur, frustra: non enim impleverunt quod voluerint, ut Christus exstingueretur; dicitur hoc enim de persecutoribus Domini, qui et in Actibus Apostolorum commemorantur (Act 4,26). 2 [v.3]. Disrumpamus links eorum, et abiiciamus a nobis iugum ipsorum. Quanquam et possit aliter íntelligi, tamen aptius ex eorum persona accipitur, quos dixit inania meditatos; ut hoc sit, Disrumpamus links eorum, et abiiciamus a nobis iugum ipsorum, dermis operam ut non nos alliget, ñeque imponatur nobis christiana religio. 3 [v.4]. Qui habitat in caelis irridebit eos, et Dominus subsannabit eos. Repetita sententia est: nam pro eo quod est, Qui habitat in caelis, subsequent positum est Dominus: et pro eo quod est, irridebit, subsequent positum est, subsannabit.

Nihil horum tamen sapere oportet carnaliter, quasi aut buccis Deus irrideat, aut naso subsannet: sed ea vis accipienda est, quam dat sanctis suis, et future cementes, id est nomen Christi et dominationem pervagaturam in posteros et universas gentes obtenturam, illos inania meditatos esse intelligant; haec enim vis qua ista praescita sunt, irrisio Dei est et subsannatio. Qui habitat in caelis, irridebit eos: cáelos si animas sanctas accipiamus, per has eos, utique praesciens quid futurum sit, deridebit Deus et subsannabit.

4 fjv.5j. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will confuse them. Demonstrating more clearly how he will speak to them, he said he will confuse them; so that when he speaks his wrath, it is in his wrath. The wrath and wrath of the Lord God must not be understood by the disturbance of the mind, but by the virtue with which he comes most justly, the creation being subject to his government. First of all, what was written in Solomon must be considered and held true: You, Lord, most powerful, judge calmly and establish us gently. Therefore the wrath of God is the affection that is engendered in the soul that knows the law of God, by contemplating the law violated by the sinner; By this affection of just souls many things are vindicated. The blindness of the mind that takes hold of those who violate the law of God can also be rightly understood by the wrath of God. 5 [v. 6 }. I have been made king by the (Lord) over Zion, his holy mountain, to preach the commandment of the Lord. It is evident that these words are said of the person of our Lord Jesus Christ. If the word Zion means, as some say, contemplation, we must understand nothing else that it represents more properly than the Church, in which every day the spirit is raised to the contemplation of the clarity of God, as the Apostle says: We, having unveiled our faces, contemplate the glory of God. Therefore the meaning is this: I have been made king by the Lord over his holy Church, which he calls a mountain because of its height and firmness. I have been made king by the (Lord), namely: I, whose chains they planned to break 4 [v.5]. Tune loquetur ad eos in ira stta, et in furore sito contuibabit eos: planius enim ostendens quomodo ad eos loquetur, dixit, conlurbabit eos; ut in ira sua, hoc sit, in furore suo. Iram autem et furorein Domini Dei non perturbationem mentis oportet intelligi, sed vim qua iustissime vindicat, subiecta sibi ad ministerium universa creatura. Pracripue namque pervidendum est et tenendum illud quod scriptum est in Salomone: Tu autem, Domine i'irtutis, cum tranquillitate judicas, et cum magna reverentia disponis nos (Wis 12,18). Ira ergo Dei est motus qui fit in anima quae legem Dei novit, cum eamdem legem videt a peccatore practeriri; per hunc enim motum iustarum animarum fines vindicantur.

I believe that in the psalm this departure was called flight because of its speed; This word is also contained in the expression of the Lord: What you have to do, do it quickly. In ordinary language we also speak in this way, so that we say: It escaped or fled from my mind, when we do not remember, and we also say of the most learned man: Nothing escapes or escapes from his mind. 4 [v. 5]. With my voice I called to the Lord; that is, not with the bodily voice, which spreads with the noise of wounded air, but with the voice of the heart, which is not heard by men, but which sounds like a cry for God. With this voice Susanna was heard, and with the same the Lord commanded that prayer be prayed without noise in closed rooms, that is, in the secrets of the heart. Without reason, someone will say that we pray on a smaller scale with this voice if no verbal sound is produced, because even being silent, when we pray in our hearts, if thoughts foreign to the affection of the prayer interpose, we cannot say: My voice cries out to God. This can only be rightly said when the soul alone, without giving access to anything carnal or human care, speaks to the Lord where He alone hears. This is called clamor for the vigor of the same vehemence. And he heard me from his holy mountain: the Lord himself is called a mountain by the prophet when he writes that it grew until it became a mountain, the stone loosened without hands. But this cannot be understood in its own right.

Then in all righteousness it is written: I fell asleep and took the dream, that is, I allowed passion in me and death followed me. And I rose, for the Lord will sustain me. In a singular way, it must be noted how in the same sentence the verb was written in the past tense and in the future; Well, it is said I got up, referring to the past, and it will sustain me being future, when I could not have risen but for that sustenance. In prophecy the past tenses are mixed very well with the future tenses in order to mean one and the other, because the things that are prophesied as coming are future in time, but due to the knowledge of those who prophesy they are already taken for granted. Likewise, verbs with present tense are also mixed, which when presented will be studied in their own place. 6 [v.7]. I will not fear the thousands of towns that surround me. In the Gospel we read of the great crowd that surrounded him during the passion and crucifixion. Arise, Lord, and save me, my God. It is not said to God who was sleeping or reclining: Get up, but it is the custom of the holy Scriptures to attribute to God what he performs in us; certainly not always, but where it can be conveniently applied; for example, when it is said that He speaks, whereas the prophets, or the apostles, or any messenger of the truth speak by His grace or gift. Hence that: Do you want to receive proof of him who speaks in me, Christ? It does not say: of him by whom I speak enlightened or helped, but rather that in absotransitur ad somnum, veluti es expergefactio qua transitur ad vigilationem. Ne pro inanibus sermonis ornamentis, repetitiones istas in divinis libris esse arbitremur. Bene ergo accipitur, Ego dormivi, et somnum cepi; Ego me passioni permisi, et mors consecuta est. Et exsurrexi, quoniam Dominus suscipiet me. Hoc magis animadvertendum est, quemadmodum in una sententia et praeteriti temporis verbum posuit, et futuri: et exsurrext enim dixit, quod est de praeterito; et suscipiet, quod est of future; cum resurgere utique nisi illa susceptione non posset. The change from the third person, where he says he heard me, to the second, when you wrote below you amplified me, if it was not done for the variety and harmony of the speech, I wonder why he wanted to indicate to men that he was first heard, and then force his hearer. Unless perhaps, having indicated how he was heard in the same dilation of the heart, he preferred to speak with God, to manifest in this way what the dilation of the heart is, that is, that he already had God infused into his heart, with whom he was internally conversing. This fits very well with the person of him who, believing in Christ, was enlightened; but I do not see how it can be consistent with that of the man-Lord himself who took the Wisdom of God, since he was never abandoned by it. But just as his prayer is rather an indication of our weakness, in the same way the Lord can speak for his faithful about the same sudden dilation of the heart, whom he also personified when he said: I was hungry, and you did not give me food; thirsty, and you gave me nothing to drink, etc. Therefore, here he can say you amplified me, as if speaking in person of one of his least ones who converses with God, who has the charity spread in his heart by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Have pity on me and hear my prayer. Why does he pray again, when he has already indicated that he was heard and dilated? Or for our sake, de niam charitas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis (Ib. 5,3.5), non habet cordis anxieties, quamvis extrinsecus a persequentibus ingerantur. Mutatio autem personae, quod a tertia, ubi ait, exaudivit, statim transit ad secundam, ubi ait, dilatasti mihi, si non varietatis ac suavitatis causa facta est, mirum cur primum tanquam indicare voluit hominibus exauditum se esse, et postea compeilare exauditorem suum. Nisi forte cum indicasset quemadmodum exauditus sit in ipsa dilatatione cordis, maluit cum Deo loqui; ut etiam hoc modo ostenderet quid sit corde dilatari, id est, iam cordi habere infusum Deum, cum quo intrinsecus colloquatur.

Although here it could also have been said that the previous sentence: Why do you love vanity and seek lies?, is written in such a way that it comes to saying: Do not love vanity and seek lies; which, said in this way, continues to be spoken most correctly: And know that the Lord has magnified his saint. But, having interposed the word diapsalma, it prevents joining this sentence with the previous one. Well, whether this word is Hebrew, as some want, which means "let it be done," or Greek, which denotes a pause or musical interval, so that psalma is the song accompanied by the psaltery, and diapsalma, the pause or silence interspersed in the song, so that just as the union of the voices in the song is called sympsalma, so their separation is called diapsalma, in which a rest appears separating what continues; I repeat that, whether it is this or that or something else, it is undoubtedly acceptable, that the sense where the diapsalm has been interposed cannot be continued or well linked. 5. The Lord will hear me when I call on him. I believe that he admonishes us here to implore God's help with great fervor, that is, with internal and spiritual love; for, as we should congratulate ourselves for enlightenment in this life, so we should pray for rest after it. Therefore, whether one speaks on behalf of the faithful who evangelizes or of the Lord himself, this verbum Domini ad illum. Quae iunctura coniunctionis, cum sententia non praecesserit cui sequens annectatur, mirabiliter fortassis insinuat prolationem veritatis in voce cum ea visione quae fit in corde esse coniunctam. Quanquam hic dici possit, quod superior sententia, Utquid diligitis vanitatem, et quaeritis mendacium? ita posita est ac si diceretur, Nolite diligere vanitatem, et quaerere mendacium; quo ita pósito, rectissima locutione sequitur: Et scitote quoniam admirableem jecit Dominus sanctum suum.

Sed interpositum diapsalma vetat istam cum superiore coniungi: sive enim hebraeum verbum sit, sicut quidam volunt, quo significatur Fiat; sive graecum, quo significatur intervallum psallendi, ut psalma sit quod psallitur, diapsalma vero interpositum in psallendo silentium; ut quemadmodum sympsalma dicitur vocum eopulatio ¡n canto, ita diapsalma disiunctio earum, ubi quaedam requies disiunctae continuationis ostenditur: sive ergo illud, sive hoc, sive aliud aliquid sit, certe illud probabile est, non recte continua et coniungi sensum, ubi diapsalma interponitur. 5. Dominus exaudiet me, dum claavero ad eum: hic nos admoneri credo, ut magna intentione cordis, id est, internal et incorporeal clamore auxilium imploremus Dei; quoniam sicut gratulandum est de illuminatione in hac vita, ita orandum pro requie post hanc vitam. Such a manner is to be taken as if it had been said: The Lord will hear you when you call upon Him. 6 [v. 5]. Be angry and do not sin. Here it may be objected: Who is worthy of being heard, or does the sinner not cry out to the Lord in vain? For the same reason, he says be angry and do not sin. This can be understood in two different ways: if you get angry, do not sin; That is to say, if this movement of the soul is awakened, since, due to the penalty of sin, it is not in your power to avoid it, at least the reason and the mind do not consent to its incentive, which was internally regenerated according to God, in such a way that if we still serve the law of sin with the flesh, with the mind we serve the law of God. Or also do penance, that is, be angry with yourself for the sins committed and stop sinning from now on. What you say in your hearts is understood, say it, so that the sentence is complete. That is, what you say in your hearts, say it; namely, do not be the people of whom it was said: Honor me with your lips, but your heart is far from me. Compungios in your beds: that is, what has already been written, in your hearts. These are the secret precincts of which the Lord admonishes that, with the doors closed, we pray within them. Compungios, or refers to the pain of penitence, so that the soul, punishing itself, may move itself to pain, so that it will not be tormented by being judged in the judgment of God; or it refers to excitement, so that, using as stimuli, we have our eyes open to contemplate the light of Christ. Many do not read compungios, but say that it should rather be read abrios, because in the Greek psalter it is aut ex persona fidelis evangelí2antis, aut ex ipsius Domini, sic accipiendum est ac si dictum sit: Dominus exaudiet vos, dum clamaveritis ad eum. 6 [v.5]. Irascimini, et nolite peccare: occurrebat enim: Quis est dignus exaudiri, aut quomodo non frustra clamat peccator ad Dominum?

Ergo Irascimini, inquit, et nolite peccare; quod duobus modis intelligi potest: aut, Etiam si irascimini, nolite peccare; id est, Etiam si surgit motus animi, qui iam propter poenam peccati non est in potestate, saltem ei non consentiat ratio et mens, quae intus regenerata est secundum Deum, ut mente serviamus legi Dei, si adhuc carne servimus legi peccati (Rom 7:25): aut, Agite poenitentiam; id est, irascimini vobis ipsis de praeteritis peccatis, et ulterius peccare desinite. Quae dicitis in cordibus vestris: subauditur, dicite; ut sit plena sententia: Quae dicitis, in cordibus vestris dicite; id est, nolite esse populus de quo dictum est: Labiis me honorant, cor autem eorum longe est a me (Is 29:13). In cubilibus vestris compungimini: hoc est quod iam dictum est, in cordibus; haec enim sunt cubilia de quibus et Dominus monet, ut intus oremus clausis ostiis (Mt 6,6). Compungitnini autem, aut ad poenitentiae dolorem refertur, ut se ipsam anima puniens compungat, ne in Dei iudicio damnata torqueatur; aut ad excitationem, ut evigilemus ad videndam luzem Christi, tanquam stimulis adhibitis. Immolate the sacrifice of righteousness and wait on the Lord. It says the same thing in another psalm: The contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God. Here it is not absurd to understand that the sacrifice of justice is that which is carried out through penance. What could be more just than to be angry at one's own sins rather than at those of others, and, punishing oneself, sacrifice to God? Or perhaps the sacrifice of justice is the righteous works that are done after penance? The diapsalma (musical silence), inserted here, perhaps with reason, also hints at the transition from the old life to the new life, so that, with the old man extinguished and weakened by penitence, it offers to God the sacrifice of justice in accordance with the regeneration of the new man when the same already purified soul is offered and immolated on the altar of faith consumed by the divine fire, that is, by the Holy Spirit, so that this is the meaning: Immolate the sacrifice of justice and wait in the Lord, that is, live righteously and wait for the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that the truth that you believed may enlighten you. 8. However, the phrase wait on the Lord was said without stating the object of the hope. And what things are expected, if not good things? But since each one tries to ask God for the good that he loves, and it is difficult to find those who love internal goods, that is, those that belong to the inner man, which mini, sed aperimini, dicunt melius legi; quoniam in graeco Psalterio est KctTocvúyriTe, quod refertur ad illam dilatationem cordis, ut excipiatur diffusio charitatis per Spiritum sanctum. 7. [v.6.7]. Sacrifice yourself sacrificium iustitiae, et wait in Domino. idem dicit in alio psalmo: Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulada (Ps 50, 19). Quare non absurde hic accipitur ipsum esse sacrificium iustitiae, quod fit per poenitentiam: quid enim iustius, quam ut suis unusquisque peccatis, quam alienis potius irascatur, seque ipsum puniens mactet Deo? An sacrificium iustitiae opera iusta sunt post poenitentiam?

Nam et interpositum diapsalma, non absurde fortassis insinuat etiam transitum de vita veteri ad vitam novam: ut-exstincto vel infirmato per poenitentiam vetere nomine, sacrificium iustitiae secundum regenerationem novi hominis offeratur Deo, cum ¡se offert ipsa anima iam abluta, et imponit in altare fidei, divina igne, id est, Spiritu sancto comprehendenda; ut iste sit sensus, Sacrifícate sacrificium iustitiae, et sperate in Domino, id est, Recte vivite, et sperate donum Spiritus sancti, ut vos veritas, cui credidistis, illustret. 8. Sed tamen Sperate in Domino, clause adhuc dictum est. Sperantur autem quae, nisi bona? Sed quia unusquisque id bonum vult a Deo impetrare quod diligit, nec facile inveniuntur qui diligant bona interiora id est, ad interiorem hominem pertinentia, quae sola diligenda sunt, cae-

They should only be loved, and the others used to meet the needs of life, not to enjoy them; admirably, after having said wait on the Lord, he added: Many say: Who will show us good things? This way of speaking and this question is everyday on the part of all the foolish and wicked, and those who long for the peace and tranquility of worldly life and who do not obtain it due to the perversity of the human race, who, blindly, dare to reproach the order of things when, pigeonholed in their own evil, they judge that the current times are worse than the past; and from those who doubt and despair of the very future life that is promised to us, who frequently say: Who knows that they are true or who came from beyond the grave to reveal these things to us? Answering the question of those who say: Who will show us good things?, he magnificently and briefly demonstrated, but only to those who see inwardly, what good things should be sought, saying: The light of your face is printed on us, O Lord! This light is everything and the true good of man, which is contemplated not with the eyes of the body, but of the mind. He said that it is imprinted on us, just as the image of the king is engraved on the denarius. Man was created in the image and likeness of God, which, by sinning, he spoiled; Its good is true and eternal if it is sculpted by being reborn. To this I believe belongs what some prudently understand about what the Lord said: Give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, when he saw Caesar's coin; which is as if he said: Just as Caesar requires of you the engraving of his image, so does God; so that, teris autem ad necessitatem utendum, non ad gaudium perfruendum; admirabiliter cum dixisset, Sperate in Domino, subiecit: Multi dicunt: Quis otendit nobis bona? Qui sermo, et quae interrogado quotidiana est omnium stultorum et iniquorum; sive pacem et tranquillitatem vitae saecularis desiderantium, et propter perversitatem generis humani non invenientium, qui etiam caeci accusare audent ordinem rerum, cum involuti meritis suis putant tempora esse peiora quam praeterita fuerunt; sive de ipsa future vita, quae nobis promittitur, dubitantium vel desperantium, qui saepe dicunt: Quis novit si vera sunt, aut quis venit ab inferís ut ist nuntiaret?

Magnifice igitur et breviter, sed intrinsecus videntibus, ostendit quae bona quaerenda sint, responders illorum interrogationi qui dicunt: Quis ostendit nobis bona? Signatum est, inquit, in nobis lumen vultus tui, Domine. Hoc lumen est totum hominis et verum bonum, quod non oculis, sed mente conspicitur. Signatum autem dixit in nobis, tanquam denarius signatur regis imagine: homo enim factus est ad imaginem et similaireinem Dei (Gen 1:26), quam peccando corruptit: bonum ergo eius est verum atque aeternum, si renascendo signetur. Et ad hoc credo pertinere, quod quidam prudenter intelligunt, illud quod Dominus viso Caesaris nummo ait: Reddite Caesari quod Caesaris est, et Deo quod Dei est (Mt 22,21); tanquam yes saysret: Quemadmodum Caesar a vobis exi-

As Caesar's coin is returned, so God's soul is returned illuminated and engraved with the light of his face. You gladdened my heart: joy should not be sought outside by those who, while still hard-hearted, love vanity and seek lies, but inside, where the light of the face of God has been engraved. Because Christ dwells in the inner man, as the Apostle says. It belongs to him to contemplate the truth, since he said: I am the truth. Also when he spoke to the Apostle, who writes: Do you want to have proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?, he certainly did not speak to him outside, but in the heart itself, that is, in that secret chamber where prayer must be prayed. 9 [v.8.9]. The men who go after temporal goods, who are undoubtedly many, were unable to say anything else except: Who will show us the goods?, when they could not see within themselves the true and certain goods. Therefore, what he adds is said of these with complete truth: Since the time of wheat, wine and its oil have multiplied. What was added is not superfluous, because there is wheat from God, since there is living bread that came down from heaven; There is wine from God, for they will be intoxicated, he says, with the abundance of their house, and there is oil from God, of which it was said you anointed my head with oil. The not a few who say: Who will show us the good things?, and who do not see that the kingdom of heaven is within them, must observe that they have multiplied since the time of wheat, wine and oil. Multiplication does not always denote abundance, git impressionem imaginis suae, sic et Deus; ut quemadmodum illi redditur nummus, sic Deo anima lumine vultus eius illustrata atque signata. Dedisti laetitiam in cor meum. Non ergo foris quaerenda est laetitia, ab his qui adhuc graves corde diligunt vaniratem et quaerunt mendacium, sed intus ubi signatum est lumen vultus Dei: in interiore enim nomine habitat Christus (Eph 3,17), ut ait Apostolus; ad ipsum enim pertinet videre veritatem, cum ille dixerit: Ego sum veritas (lo 14,6). Et cum loquebatur in Apostólo dicente: An vultis experimentum eius accipere qui in me loquilur Christus? (II Cor 13,3). Non ei foris utique; thirst in ipso corde, id est, in illo cubili ubi orandum est (Mt 6,6), loquebatur. 9 [v.8.9]. Sed nomines temporalia sectantes, qui certe multi sunt, nihil aliud noverunt dicere, nisi Quis otendit nobis bona? cum vera et certa bona intra semetipsos videre non possint.

Itaque consequenter of his rectissime dicitur, quod adiungit: A tempore frumenti, vini et olei sui multiplicati sunt. Non enim vacat, quod additum est, sui: est enim et frumentum Dei, siquidem est pañis vivus qui de cáelo descendit (lo 6,51); est et vinum Dei, nam Inebriabuntur, inquit, ab ubertate domus tuae (Ps 35,9) est et oleum Dei, de quo dictum est: Impinguasti in oleo caput meum (Ps 22,5). Isti autem multi qui dicunt, Quis otendit nobis bona? et regnum caelorum intra se esse non vident (Lk 17,21), a tempore frumenti, vini et olei sui multiplicati sunt. Non enim multiplied semper ubertatem significat, et non plerumque exiguitatem: cum dedita tem-

because it often designates scarcity. The soul given over to temporal pleasures continually burns with desires that it cannot satisfy, and, filled with multiple and ruinous thoughts, they do not allow it to contemplate the simple good; such is that of which it is said: The corruptible body impregnates the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the reason that thinks many things. This soul, due to the access and recess of temporal goods, since the time of wheat, wine and oil, is so increased and filled with innumerable imaginations, that it cannot put into practice what is precepted: Feel good about the Lord and seek Him with simplicity of heart. This multiplicity is vehemently opposed to that simplicity, and, therefore, the faithful man, having abandoned these, who in reality are many and who, no doubt increased by the desire for temporal goods, say: Who will show us the goods?, which should not be sought outside with the eyes of the flesh, but within, with simplicity of heart, rejoices and says: In peace I will sleep in it and take the dream. The complete alienation of the mind from obsolete things and the oblivion of the calamities of the world are rightly expected by such, which, under the name of somnolence and sleep, decorously and prophetically designates the place where the utmost peace cannot be interrupted by any disturbance. But this is no longer possessed in this life, but must be expected in the next. This is demonstrated by the same words, since the future tense is used, since it was not said: I slept deeply and took the dream, or I sleep and take the dream, but I will sleep deeply and take the dream. So this corrupporalibus voluptatibus anima semper exardescit cupiditate, nec satiari potest, et multiplici atque aerumnosa cogitatione disienta, simplex bonum videre non sinitur; qualis est illa de qua dicitur: Corpus enim, quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum plana cogitantem (Wis 9,15). Talis anima temporalium bonorum decessione et successione, id est, a tempore frumenti, vini et olei sui, innumerabilibus complete phantasmatibus sic multiplicata est, ut non possit agere quod praeceptum est: Sentite de Domino in bonitote, et in simplicitate cordis quaerite illum (Ib. 1,1); ist enim multiplicitas illi simplicitati vehementer adversa est.

Et ideo istis relictis qui multi sunt, multiplicati scilicet temporalium cupiditate et dicunt, Quis ostendit nobis bona? quae non oculis foris, sed intus cordis simplicitate quaerenda sunt, vir fidelis exsultat et dicit: In pace, in idipsum obdormiam, et so? nnum capiam. Recte enim speratur a talibus omnimoda mentís abalienatio a mortal ¡bus rebus et miseriarum saeculi huius oblivio, quae nomine obdormitionis et somni decenter et prophetice significatur, ubi summa pax nullo tumultu interpellari potest. Sed hoc iam tenetur in hac vita, sed post hanc vitam sperandum est. Hoc etiam ipsa verba ostendunt, quae futuri sunt temporis: non enim dictum est, aut, Obdormivi et somnum cepi; aut, Obdormio et somnum capio; sed, Obdormiam et somnum capiam. lukewarm will put on incorruption, and this mortal will put on immortality; then death will be swallowed up to become victory. This is why it is said: If we strive for what we do not see, we wait patiently. 10 [v. 10]. Therefore, he conveniently adds lastly, and says: For you, O Lord, in a special way have made me dwell in hope. He did not say here: you will do, but you did. In the one where this hope exists, what is hoped for will undoubtedly exist. He appropriately says in a singular way, which can be taken in contrast to those many who, increased since the time of wheat, wine and their oil, say: Who will show us good things? This multiplicity perishes and this unity subsists in the saints, of whom it is said in the Apostolic Acts: The multitude of believers had one soul and one heart. Therefore, if we wish to adhere and be one with God our Lord, we must be singular and simple, that is, lovers of eternity and unity, and distance ourselves from the multitude and the mob of beings that are born and die.

1 [v. l]. The title of the psalm is: In favor of her who receives the inheritance. Hoc est unde dicitur: Si autem quod non videmus speramus, per patientiam exspectamus (Rom 8,25). 10 [v.10]. Singulares ergo et simplices, id est, secreti a multitudine ac turba nascentium rerum ac morientium, amatores aetemitatis et unitatis esse debenmus, si uni Deo et Domino nostro cupimus inhaerere.
