tured, according to that: Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the earth. What land, if not that of which it is said: You are my hope and my portion in the land of the living?; and the following and clearer: The Lord is the part of my inheritance and my cup. In turn, the Church is called the inheritance of God, according to that: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as an inheritance. Therefore God is our inheritance, because he feeds and preserves us, and we are God's inheritance, because he administers and governs us. Therefore, in this psalm the voice of the Church is heard, called to the inheritance so that it becomes an inheritance of the Lord. 2 [v. 2]. Oh Lord! Hear my voice: call, invoke the Lord so that, helping her, she may leave aside the evil of this century and come to Him. Understand my cry: admirably demonstrate what this cry must reach God, born from the secret chamber of the heart, without bodily noise, since the bodily voice is heard, but the spiritual one is understood. This is the hearing of God, hearing not with carnal ears, but by the presence of his majesty. 3 [v. 3]. Listen to the voice of my prayer, that is, to the voice that asks God to understand. What is this? He already hinted at it when he said: Understand my cry. Hear the voice of my prayer, my King and my God. Although the Son is God, and God is the Father, and together the Father and the Son are one God; and if we inquire about the Holy Spirit, we will not say anything other than that He is God, and if we name at the same time the Father, the Son rens beata sit secundum illud: Beati mites, quia ipsi haereditate possidebunt terram (Mt 5,4); quam rerram? nisi de qua dicitur: Spes mea es tu, portio mea in ierra vivostium (Ps 141,6); et illud manifestius: Dominus pars haereditatis jneae et calicis mei (Ps 15,5). Dicitur et haereditas Dei vicissim Ecclesia secundum illud: Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes haereditatem tuam (Ps 2,8). Ergo haereditas nostra Deus dicitur, quia ipse nos pascit et continet: et haereditas Dei dicimur, quia ipse nos administrat et regit. Quapropter vox Ecclesiae est in hoc psalmo vocatae ad haereditatem, ut et ipsa fiat haereditas Domini. 2 [v.2]. Verba mea exaudí, Domine: vocata invoket Dominum, ut eodem opitulante pertranseat nequitiam saeculi huius, et ad eum perveniat.

Intellige clamorem meum: bene otendit quis iste sit clamor, quam interior de cordis cubili sine strepitu corporis perveniat ad Deum; quandoquidem vox corporalis auditur, spiritualis autem intelligitur. Quanquam hoc sit etiam exaudiré Dei, non aure carnali, sed maestatis praesentia. 3 [v.3]. Intenie voci obsecrationis meae: id est, illi voci, quam ut Deus intellígat petit; quae qualis sit iam insinuavit, cum dixit: Intellige clamorem meum. lntende voci obsecrationis meae, Rex meus et Deus meus. Quamvis et Filius Deus, et Pater Deus, et simul Pater et Filius unus Deus; et si interrogemur de Spiritu sancto, nihil aliud responderdum est, nisi quod Deus sit; et cum simul dicuntur Pater et Filius et

and the Holy Spirit, we must understand that he is one God; However, Scripture usually calls the Son king. Then, according to what is written: Through me he goes to the Father, rightly he calls himself first my King and then my God. However, he did not say attend, but attend, since the Catholic faith does not teach that there are two or three gods, but that the Trinity is one God, nor that at the same time the same Trinity can at some time be Father, in another Son and in another Holy Spirit, as Sabellius stated, but that the Father is nothing more than Father, the Son is nothing more than Son and the Holy Spirit is nothing more than Holy Spirit, and this Trinity is only one God. When the Apostle said: from Him, through Him and in Him all things, he is believed to have insinuated the same Trinity, and yet he did not add: to them the glory, but to Him the glory. 4 f_v.4}. For I will pray to you, Lord, in the morning you will hear my voice. What does it mean that he previously said: Hear, as if he longed to be heard at once, and now he does not say: Hear, but in the morning you will hear, and likewise he does not say: I pray to you, but to you I will pray, and then he does not write: I am present and I will see, but in the morning I will be present and I will see, but his previous prayer is the same invocation? Finding himself in the dark among the storms of this world, he realizes that he does not see what he wants, and yet he does not lose hope, because the hope that is seen is not hope. However, he understands the reason for not seeing: the night has not yet passed, that is, the darkness that the sins deserved. Therefore, he says I will pray to you, Lord, that is, so great are you, to whom Spiritus sanctus, nihil aliud intelligendum est quam unus Deus; tamen regem Fiüum solent appellare Scripturae. Secundum ergo illud quod dictum est, Per me itur ad Patrem (lo 14,6), recte primo, Rex meus, et deinde, Deus meus. Nec tamen dixit, Intendite; sed, Intende: non enim duos aut tres déos fides catholica praedicat, sed ipsam Trinitatem unum Deum: non ut eadem Trinitas simul possit aliquando Pater, aliquando Filius, aliquando Spiritus sanctus dici, sicut Sabellius credidit; sed ut Pater nonnisi Pater, et Filius nonnisi Filius, et Spiritus sanctus nonnisi Spiritus sanctus, et haec Trinitas nonnisi unus Deus. Quia et cum dixisset Apostolus: Ex quo omnia, per quem omnia, in quo omnia (Rom 11:36), Trinitatem ipsam insinuasse creditur; nec tamen subiecit, Ipsis gloria; thirst, Ipsi glory.

I will pray that in the morning you will hear my voice. You are not, he says, that you can be seen by those whose eyes the night of sins has not yet departed from; But, once the night of my error has passed and the darkness in which I enveloped myself due to my sins has vanished, you will hear my voice. You will destroy all those who speak lies, because they are contrary to the truth. But so that no one thinks that there is any substance or nature contrary to the truth, understand that lies belong to things that do not exist. If you say what it is, you say the truth; If you say what is not, you say a lie. Therefore he says: You will destroy all those who speak lies, because, turning away from what is, they turn to what is not. Many lies appear to have been told not out of malice, but out of kindness in favor of someone's health or good, such as those of the midwives, of whom it is said in the Exodus that they announced what was false to Pharaoh so that the children of the Israelites would not be killed. These are not praised for the fact that they are lies, but for the intention, because those who only lie in this way sometimes deserve to be excused from all lies. Lies of this kind are not found in the perfect, and to them it was said: Let your speech be yes, yes; no no; What happens from this comes from the evil one. Nor was it written without reason elsewhere: The mouth that lies kills the soul, so that no one thinks that the perfect and spiritual man must strive in favor of this temporal life, since by this temporal death the soul is not killed: neither his own nor that of his neighbor. But since it is one thing to lie and another to hide the truth, just as it is one thing to tell falsehood and another to keep silent about the truth, if someone perhaps does not want to hand over a man to this temporary death, he must be prepared to hide the truth, but not to say something that is not valid. There are only two types of lies that do not imply a serious fault; However, they are not without sin: when we joke or when we lie to do good. In the first case, that is, in joking, the lie is not harmful because it does not deceive, since the person to whom it is said knows that it was said in a joking sense. In the second it is more bearable, because not a little benevolence would enter. What does not have a double meaning should not be said to be a lie, as, for example, if someone has been given a sword and promises to return it when the person who gave it asks for it; But if he, deranged, demands his sword, it is evident that he should not return it to him, so that he does not kill himself or others until he regains his senses. Here there is no double heart, because the one to whom the sword was given when he promised to deliver it to the petitioner did not think that he could demand it when he was deranged. The Lord hid the truth when he said to his disciples, unable to understand it: I have many things to tell you, but now you cannot bear them; and the apostle Saint Paul when saying: I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people. The same story from which the prophet took the mysterious veil will not be considered in this psalm. If we have already passed on to Jesus Christ, let us remove the veil. And first of all let's ask what meaning the names of the characters have. There was no shortage of interpreters who, investigating the meaning of these names in a spiritual sense, not in a carnal one, announced to us that Cusi means silence; Jemini, right; Aquitophel, brother's ruin. Through these interpretations, that traitor Judas once again comes to meet us, so that Absalom is his image, insofar as his name is interpreted as peace of the father. The father showed himself to be a peacemaker towards him, although he carried war in his heart due to his deceptions, as was discussed in the exposition of Psalm 3. On the other hand, just as it is found in the Gospel that the disciples are called children of our Lord Jesus Christ, it is also found in the same Gospel that they are called brothers, for upon resurrecting the Lord says: Go and tell my brothers; The Apostle also calls him Firstborn among many brothers. Then the ruin of his disciple who handed him over is rightly understood as the ruin of the Brother, which, as we said, means the word Achitophel. By translating Cusi by silence, it is rightly understood that our Lord fought against those deceptions with silence, that is, that the blindness that took place on the part of Israel when persecuting the Lord so that the fullness of the people could enter and thus all Israel would be saved, was carried out with the highest secrecy. When the Apostle arrived at this highest secret and deepest silence he exclaimed, instruebat. Sed quoniam non ipsa historia in hoc psalmo considerada est de qua Propheta mysteriorum velamen assumpsit, si transitum ad Christum fecimus, auferatur velamen (2 Cor 3:16). Et primo ipsorum nominum significationem interrogemus quid sibi velit. Non enim defuerunt interpretes qui haec ipsa non carnaliter ad litteram, sed spiritualíter investigantes, edicerent nobis quod Chusi interprétete Silentium; lemini autem, Dexter; Achitophel, Fratris ruin. Quibus interpretationibus rursum nobis traditor ille ludas occurrit, ut Abessalon eius imaginem gestet, secundum quod Patris pax interpretatur; quia pacatus erga illum exstitit pater, quamvis ipse dolis suis bellum haberet in corde, sicut in psalmo tertio tractatum est.

Quemadmodum autem invenitur in Gospel filios Domini nostri Iesu Christi dictos esse disciples (Mt 9:14), sic in eoderm Gospel invenitur etiam fratres esse appellatos; resurgens enim Dominus ait: Vade, et dic jratribus tneis (lo 20,17), et Apostolus eum dicit primogenitum in multis fratribus (Rom 8,29): discipuli ergo eius ruina qui eum tradidit, recte intelligitur Fratris ruina, quod Achitophel interpret diximus. Chusi autem, quod interpretatur Silentium, recte accipitur adversus illos dolos Dominum nostrum silentio dimicasse, id est altissimo secreto quo caecitas ex parte Israel facta est, eum Dominum persequebantur, ut plenitudo Gentium subintraret, et sic omnis Israel salvus ieront. In the face of infidels and persecutors, that is silence and secrecy; before his own, to whom it was said: I no longer call you servants, because the servant does not know what his Lord is doing; I have called you friends, because I have revealed to you all the things that I have heard from my Father; That is, before his friends there is no silence, but words of silence, that is, an exposed and clear reason for that silence. This silence, that is, Cusi, who is the son of Jemini, that is, of the right, was not to be hidden from the saints, since it was done for them. And yet he says: Let the left hand ignore what the right hand does. Sing, then, the perfect soul in prophecy to whom that secret was made known because of the words of Cusi, that is, because of the knowledge of it O altitudo divitiarum sapientiae et scientiae Dei, quam inscrutabilia sunt iudicia eius, et investigabiles viae ipsius! Quis enim cognovitmentem Domini, aut quis consiliarius Ulitis Fuit? (Rom 11,33.34) ita magnum illud silentium non expositione magis aperit, quam admiratione commendat. Hoc silentio Dominus sacramentum venerabilis passionis occultans, voluntarym ruinara fratris, id est, nefarium scelus traditoris sui, in suae misericordiae atque providentiae ordinem vertit; ut quod ille ad perniciem unius hominis perversa mente faciebat, iste ad salutem omnium hominum provida gubernatione conferret. Cantat ergo Psalmum Domino anima perfection, quae iam dignified est nosse secretum Dei; cantat pro verbis Chusi, quia meruit nosse verba illius silentii.

Apud infideles enim et persecutors, silentium est illud atque secretum: apud suos autem, quibus dictum est, Iam non dico vos servos, quia servus nescit quid faciat Dominus eius; vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quae audi a Patre meo, note feci vobis (lo 15,15): apud amicos ergo eius non est silentium, sed verba silentii, id est, ratio expósita et manifesta illius silentii. Quod silentium, id est Chusi, dicitur íilius Iemini, id est dextri: non enim abscondendum erat sanctis quod pro illis gestum est. Et tamen Nesciat, inquit, sinistra quid faciat dextra (Mt 6,3). Canit ergo anima perfection in prophetia, cui secretum illud innotuit, pro verbis Chusi, id est pro cognitione eiusdem secreti; quod secretum dexter Deus, id est favens atque pro-
Deprecation of a slandered righteous man

secret. This secret was done by the upright or right God, favoring and being propitious (to David). Therefore this silence is called the son of right, that is, Cusi, son of Jemini. 2 [v.2.3]. O Lord, my God, I have hoped in you; Save me from all those who persecute me and deliver me. As a perfect person who only needs to defeat the envious devil, having overcome all strife and contrariety of vices, he says: Save me from all those who persecute me and deliver me, lest he, like a lion, at some time snatch my soul. The Apostle says: The devil, your adversary, goes around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour. Having used the plural when saying: Save me from all those who persecute me, he then uses the singular, saying: lest at any time he snatch my soul like a lion; He does not say lest at some time they will take away, knowing what enemy would remain and how staunch an adversary he is to the perfect soul. Since there is no one to redeem and no one to save, that is, lest he take away if you do not redeem and save; because if God does not redeem or save, he snatches away. 3 [v.4.5]. And to show that the already perfect soul says this, by which the fraudulent schemes of only the devil must be avoided, pay attention to what follows: Oh Lord, my God!, yes I did this. What do you mean when you say this? Perhaps it is a universal sin, since it does not give the name of the sin? If such a meaning does not please us, let us understand that what follows was said as if we had asked what meaning the word this has, and answers: Si hay pitius ei, operatus est: quare hoc silentium Filius dextri appellatur, quod est Chusi, jüii Iemini? 2 [v.2.3]. Domine Deus ineus, in te speravi; salvum me jac ex omnibus persequentibus me, et eripe me. Tanquam cui non restat iam perfection nisi invidus diabolus, superato omni bello atque adversitate vitiorum, dicit: Salvum me jac ex ómnibus persequentibus me, et eripe me: nequando rapiat ut leo animam meam. Dicit Apostolus: Aiversarius vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quaerens quem devoret (1 Petr 5,8). Itaque cum diceret per pluralem numerum: Salvum me jac ex ómnibus persequentibus me, singularem postea intulit dices, nequando rapiat ut leo animam meam: non enim ait, nequando rapiant, sciens quis restiterit inimicus, et perfection animae vehementer adversus. Dum non est qui redeemat, ñeque qui salvum jaciat: id est, ne ille rapiat, dum tu non redeemís ñeque salvum facis; si enim Deus non redeemimat ñeque salvum faciat, ille rapit. 3 [v.4.5].

Et ut manifestum sit iam perfection animam hoc dicere, cui solius diaboli fraudulentissimae insidiae cavendae sunt, vide quid sequatur: Domine Deus tneus, si jeci istud. Quid est quod vocat istud? an quia non dicit nomen peccati, universale peccatum intelligendum est? Qui intellectus si displicet, illud accipiamus dici quod sequitur: tanquam si interrogassemus, Quid est hoc quod dicis, istud? respond: If it is iniS.Ag. 19

iniquity in my hands. The rest: If I returned evils to those who repaid me, it is evident that it refers to all sin, because only the perfect can truly say it. For the Lord says: Be perfect like your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil and rains on the just and the unjust; Therefore he who does not return evil for evil is perfect. Therefore, when the perfect soul prays because of the words of Cushí, son of Jemini, that is, because of the knowledge of that secret and silence that the Lord, propitious and merciful with us, carried out for our health, patiently tolerating and enduring the lies of his betrayer, let him (the Lord) say to this perfect soul, exposing the reason for the same secret: I endured my betrayer with great silence and patience for you, impious and sinner, to may your iniquities be washed away with the shedding of my blood; Therefore, will you not imitate me, not returning evil for evil? Noting and understanding what the Lord did in his favor and taking advantage of his example to perfect himself, he says: If I returned evil for evil, that is, if I did not do what you taught me by working, then I will fall without hope under my enemies. And with reason he did not say whether I repaid evils to those who gave me, but to those who repaid me evils. He who gives back has already received something before. The man who does not return evils to him who, having received goods, returns evils for goods shows greater patience than if he had intended to harm without having received any benefit. Then if I repaid, he says to those who repaid me evils, that is, if I did not imitate you in that silence.

That is, in the patience that you endured for me, I fell, therefore, without hope under my enemies. He who, being a man, wishes to take revenge on man boasts of himself in vain, because when he tries to publicly defeat man, he is secretly defeated by the devil. Frivolous effect, vain and arrogant joy, because he could hardly be defeated. This understands where the greatest victory is achieved and where the Father, who sees in the hidden, rewards. Therefore, in order not to return evil for evil, he who is instructed in the holy Scripture, in which it is written: Better is he who conquers wrath than he who takes a city, rather he conquers wrath than man. If I repaid evils to those who repaid me, then I will fall hopelessly under my enemies. In this he seems to be swearing by cursing, which is the most serious kind of oath, which takes place when a man says: if I did this, let me suffer this. But one thing is the action of swearing in the mouth of the one who swears, and another in the meaning of the one who prophesies. Here he says what must happen as certain to men who repay evils to those who repay evils; not that he desires something for himself or for another as with an oath.

you remove in manibus meis. Iam ergo manifestum est de omni peccato dici Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala; quod non potest veré dicere nisi perfectus. Ait quippe Dominus: Estote perfecti, sicut Pater vester qui est in caelis, qui solem suum oriri facit super bonds et malas, et pluit super iustos et iniustos (Mt 5,48.45); qui ergo non reddit retribuentibus mala perfectus est. Cum ¡taque oret perfect anima pro verbis Chusi, jilü lernini, id est pro cognitione illius secreti atque silentii, quod pro salute nostra operatus est propitius nobis et misericors Dominus, ut toleraret et patientissime sustineret dolos traditoris sui: tanquam huic perfection animae dicat, exposens rationem ipsius secreti: Ego pro te impío et peccatore, ut tuae iniquitates mej sanguinis effusione lavaentur, magno silentio et magna patientia traditorem meum pertuli, nonne imitaberis me, ut et tu non reddas mala pro malis? animadvertens igitur et intelligens quid pro illo fecerit Dominus, et eius exemplo ad perfectionem proficiens, dicit: Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, id est, si non feci quod tu fazando docuisti, decidam ergo ab inimicis meis inanis. Et bene non ait, Si reddidi tribuentibus mihi mala, sed, retribuentibus: qui enim retribuit, iam aliquid acceperat; maioris autem patientiae est, nec ei mala rependere qui acceptis beneficiis reddit mala pro bonis, quam si nullo ante accepto benefit nocere voluisset, Si reddidi ergo, inquit, retribuentibus mihi mala, id est, si fe ion imitatus surn in ¡lio silentio, fjoc es t

patientia tua quam pro me operatus es, decidam ab inimicis meis inanis. Inaniter enim se iactat, qui cum et ipse homo sit, cupit se de nomine vindicare: et cum superare hominem palam quaerit, occulte a diabolo superatur, inanis effectus vana et superba laetitia, quod quasi vinci non potuit. Intelligit ergo iste ubi maior fiat victoria, et ubi Pater reddat qui videt in occulto. Ne reddat ¡taque retribuentibus mala, iram potius quam hominem vincit, illis etiam litteris eruditus, in quibus scriptum est: Aíelior est qui vincit iram, quam qui capit civitatem (Prov 16:32, sec. 70). Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, decidam ergo ab inimicis meis inanis. Iurare videtur per exsecrationem, quod est gravissimum iurisiurandi genus, cum homo dicit: Si illud feci, illud patiar. Be aliud est iuratio in ore iurantis, aliud in significatione prophetantis: hic enim dicit quid veré contingat hominibus qui reddunt retribuentibus mala; non quod sibi, aut alicui, quasi iureiurando imprecetur.

4 [v. 6]. So let the enemy pursue my soul and capture it. Naming the enemy again in the singular, he very patently declares the one whom he previously called a lion. He pursues the soul, and if he deceives it, he takes possession of it. Men are cruel until they kill the body, but after this visible death they cannot take possession of the soul; but the devil will possess the souls that he captured in pursuit. And trample my life into the earth, that is, and, trampling, turn my life into earth, that is, into your food;

4 [v.6]. Persequatur ergo inimicus animam meam, et comprehendat. Iterum inimicum singulari numero nominans, illum magis magisque minifestat quem superius velut leonem appellavit. Ipse enim animam persequitur; et si deceperit, comprehendet. Nam nomines usque ad interfectionem corporis saeviunt, animam vero post istam visibilem mortem in potestate 'habere non possunt; diabolus autem quas animas persecutus

for he not only called a lion, but also a serpent, to whom it was said: Thou shalt eat earth; and also to sinful man it was said: You are earth and to earth you will go. And reduce my glory to dust. This is that dust that the wind throws on the face of the earth, that is, the vain, the absurd, the inflated and not solid boasting of the proud, which is like a balloon inflated with dust by the wind. No wonder he said glory here, because he does not want it to be reduced to dust. He wants to have it solid in conscience before God, where there is no boasting. He who boasts, writes the Apostle, let him glory in God. This solidity is reduced to dust if anyone, despising out of pride the secrets of conscience, where only God tests man, wants to boast before men. Hence what is said elsewhere: God will crush the bones of those who please men. Whoever learned well or knew the degrees of the vices that must be overcome, understands that this vice of vain glory is the only or the most important one that must be avoided by the perfect; for the vice by which the soul first fell, is the last one that overcomes the soul: The beginning of all sin is pride. And the beginning of man's pride is apostasy from God. 5 [v.7]. Arise, Lord, in your anger. Why does this one we call perfect still provoke God to anger? Is it not clear that he is rather perfect who, when he was stoned, said: Lord, do not impute this sin to them? Or is it that he does not ask these things for men, but for the devil and his angels, who

possess sinful and impious men? Everyone who prays does not pray out of anger against man, but out of compassion, so that this possession may be taken from the devil by the Lord, who justifies the wicked. When the wicked is justified, from wicked he becomes righteous, and from the possession of the devil he becomes the temple of God; But since it is a punishment for the possession in which he wishes to dominate to be taken away from someone, that is why he calls this punishment the wrath of God against the devil, since he stops possessing what he possessed. Arise, Lord, in your anger: here, apparently, he said arise in a human and mysterious sense, as if God were sleeping, while he lives hidden in his secrets. Exalt yourself in the terms of my enemies. He called the same possession terms where he rather wants God to be exalted, that is, honored and glorified, than the devil, when the wicked are justified and praise God. Arise, O Lord my God, in the precept that you commanded; That is, show yourself humble, because you prescribed humility, and you first fulfill what you commanded, so that by your example, overcoming pride, they may not be possessed by the devil, who advised pride against your precepts, saying: Eat and your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods.

Et conculcet in terram vham meam: id est conculcando, terram faciat vitam meam, cibum •scilicet suum; non enim tantum leo, sed etiam serpens appellatus est, cui dictum est: 1'erratn manducabis; et peccatori homini dictum est, Terra es, et in terram ibis (Gen 3,14.19). And glory meam in pulverem deducat. Hic est ilie pulvis, quem proiicit ventus a facie terrae, superborum scilicet vana et inepta iactantia, et inflata non solidata, tanquam vento elatus pulveris globus. Recte ¡taque hic possuit gloriam, quam non vult in pulverem deduci. Vult enim eam solidam habere in conscientia coram Deo, ubi nuüa iactantia est; Qui gloriatur, inquit, in Domino glorietur (1 Cor 1:31). Ista soliditas in pulverem deducitur, si per superbiam quisque contemnens secreta conscientiae, ubi solus Deus hominem probat, velit apud nomines gloriari; Hinc est quod alibi dicit: Deus conteret ossa placentium hominibus (Ps 52,6). Qui autem faene didicit vel expertus est vitiorum superandorum gradus, intelligit hoc vitium inanis gloriae, vel solum, vel máxime cavendum esse perfectis: quo primo enim vitio lapsa est anima, hoc ultimum vincit. hiitium autem omnis peccati superbia; et, lnitium superbiae hominis, I will apostatize to Deo (Eccli 10,15.14).

5 [v.7]. Exsurge, Domine, in ira tua. Quid adhuc iste quem perfectum dicimus, ad iram provocat Deum? Nonne videndum est ne potius ille perfectus sit, qui cum lapidaretur, dixit: Domine, ne statues lilis hoc peccatum? (Act 7,59). An et iste, non adversus homines haec precatur,

6 [v.8]. Et congregatio populorum circumdabit te. Duplex intellectus est. Congregatio enim populorum, sive credentium, sive persequentium potest accipi, quorum utrumque eadem Domini nostri humilitate factum est: quam contemnens persequentium multitudo, circumdedit eum, de qua dic-

or [v.8}. The congregation of the people will surround you. This has a double meaning, because the congregation of the people can be taken for that of the believers or that of the persecutors. These two classes are constituted by the same humility of our Lord Jesus Christ. So the multitude of those who persecuted him

They guide him, despising him, and surrounded him; It was said of her: Why do the nations roar and the people meditate on vain things? The multitude of believers surrounded him because of his humility, in such a way that it could be said with great reason: The blindness on the part of Israel was suitable for the fullness of the nations to enter; and that: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession. And through this he returns to the top, that is, through this congregation he returns to the top; which is understood to have been done by resurrecting and returning to heaven. Thus, being glorified, he gave the Holy Spirit which he could not give before his glorification, as it is read in the Gospel: The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. Having returned to heaven because of the gathering of the people, he sent the Holy Spirit, with which, filling the preachers of the Gospel, they populated the world with churches. 7. The words arise, Lord, in your anger; exalt yourself in the terms of my enemies, they can also have this meaning: arise in your anger and my enemies do not understand you; so that to exalt is to put on high so that you are not understood, which refers to silence. About this exaltation it is said in another psalm: And he ascended upon the cherub and flew. And he made darkness his hiding place. Because of this exaltation, that is, because of this concealment, as those who are to crucify you do not know you for their sins, the congregation of believers will surround you. By the same humility he is exalted, that is, he is not known; so that this is what he says next refers to: And arise, O Lord my God, in the precept that you commanded; that is, when you appear tum est, Quare jremuerunt gentes, et populi meditati sunt inania? (Ps 2,1) credentium autem per eius humilitatem multitudo ita eum circumdedit, ut verissime diceretur, Caecitas ex parte Israel ¡acta est, ut plenitudo Gentium intraret (Rom 11,25); et illud, Postula a me, et dabo tibí gentes haereditatem tuam, et possessionem tuam terrae terms (Ps 2,8). Et propter hanc in altum regredere: id est, propter hanc congregationem regredere in altum; quod resurgendo et in caelum ascending fecisse intelligitur. Ita enim glorifkatus dedit Spiritum sanctum, qui ante glorificationem eius dari non posset, sicut in Gospel positum est: Spiritus autem nondum erat datus, quia Iesus nondum erat clarificatus (lo 7,39).

Regressus ergo in altum propter congregationem populorum, misit Spiritum sanctum; quo impleti praedicatores Evangelii orbem terrarum Ecclesiis impleverunt. 7. Potest et sic iste sensus intelligi: Exsurge, Domine, in ira tua, exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum: id est, exsurge in ira tua, et non te intelligant inimici mei; ut hoc sit exaltare, id est, altus efficere ne intelligaris, quod refertur ad illud silentium. Sic enim de hac exaltatione in alio psalmo dicitur: Et ascendit super Cherubin, et volavit. Et posit tenebras latibulum suum (Ps 17,11.12): qua exaltatione, id est occultatione, cum te merit peccatorum suorum non intellexerint qui te crucifigent, congregatio credentium circumdabit te. humble, be tall, so that my enemies do not understand. Sinners are enemies of the righteous, and the wicked, of the pious. Then it is rightly said: and for the sake of this congregation he returns on high; That is to say, set yourself aside again to the height of your secrets for this congregation of peoples who own your name and do not execute your deeds. 8. Whether this is the most convenient exposition or the previous one, without prejudice to another, better or equal, made by another, it very opportunistically follows: The Lord judges the people. Because if it is understood that he returned to heaven, when after the resurrection he ascended to heaven, he appropriately continues: the Lord judges the people because from there he will come to judge the living and the dead, and the same if we understand it in such a way that he returns to heaven, when the knowledge of the truth abandons sinful Christians, because of the same coming it was said: Do you think that when the Son of man comes he will find him on the earth? The Lord judges the people. What Lord but Jesus Christ? The Father does not judge anyone; He left all judgment in the hands of the Son. Notice how, for this reason, this soul that perfectly prays does not fear the day of judgment, and truly with sure desire says in prayer: Your kingdom come; Then judge me, he says, O Lord, according to my justice. In the previous psalm the sick man begged, imploring God's mercy rather than remembering some of his merits, because the Son of God came to call sinners to penitence. So, then, he said there: Lord, save me by your mercy, that is, not by virtue of my merits; but now in this psalm, as he has been called and retained and observed the precepts that he received, does he dare ab omnium pravarum opinionum labe purgata? Non ergo immerito dicitur, Et propter hanc congregationem in altum regredere; id est, secede rursus in altitudinem secretorum tuorum, etiam propter hanc congregationem populorum quae habet nomen tuum et facta tua non facit. 8. How can the righteous be guided, if not within, since for those things that in the beginning of Christian times appeared worthy of admiration to men, the saints were still tormented by the persecution of worldly men, and now, after the Christian name began to be in the highest concept, hypocrisy grew, that is, the simulation of those who prefer under the Christian name to please men more than God? In what way, I repeat, is the righteous person guided among so much confusion of deception, if not when God searches the hearts and loins, seeing the thoughts of all? These thoughts are symbolized in the name of the heart and the delights under the name of the kidneys. The delight of temporal and earthly things is rightly attributed to the kidneys, because this part is the most inferior part of man, and the region where the pleasure of carnal generation resides, through which human nature is transmitted in this calamitous life and deceptive joy through the succession of offspring. Then, God searches our heart and sees with his gaze that it is there where our treasure is, that is, it is Filius Dei. l.fv-l]The text of this psalm does not speak at all about winepresses. However, due to many and diverse similarities, one and the same thing is often suggested in the Holy Scriptures. By wine presses we can understand the churches, for the same reason that we also understand the era of the Church. In the threshing floor and in the winepress, all that is done is cleaning the fruit from its wrappings, which were necessary for the harvest and the grapes to be born, grow and mature. After these, whether wrappers or peduncles, that is, from these straws, the grains are stripped on the threshing floor, and from this residue the wine is released in the winepress, just as in the churches they are separated with spiritual love, by the work of the ministers of God, the good from the multitude of worldly men, who are gathered together with the good, however, first for these, that multitude is necessary, in order to be born and become fit for the divine word. This division is also carried out now, but not materially, but by affection the good are separated from the bad, although they coexist in the Church at the same time in terms of bodily presence. Another time will come in which the grains will be separated into the barns and the wine will be separated into the cellar, for it says that it will lock the grains in the barns and burn the chaff with an inextinguishable game. If it had been written in this way: what is man that you remember him and the son of man, since you visit him, the word man would appear repeated; but when the man or the son of man is recorded, the difference is clearly hinted at. Without hesitation it must be understood that every son of man is a man, although it cannot be understood that every man is a son of man: Adam is certainly a man, but not a son of man. For this reason it is already allowed to consider and distinguish what difference there is in this place between man and the son of man. Those who bear the image of the earthly man, who is not the son of man, are represented under the name of men, and those who bear the image of the celestial man are rather called sons of men. The former is called the old man, the latter the new; but the new is born from the old, because spiritual regeneration begins with the change of earthly and worldly life, and, therefore, this one is called the son of man. The man in this place is the earth, and the son of man, the heavenly. In this way he wants it to be understood that all things are subject to our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not except any. However, when he says: All the sheep and the oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea that travel the paths of the sea, he does not seem to have added anything extraordinary. For it seems that, having left aside the celestial virtues, the powers, and all the armies of angels, and even men themselves, he only subjected the animals to him, unless by sheep and oxen we understand the holy souls, either bearing fruits of innocence or already working so that the earth may bear fruit, that is, so that earthly men may regenerate themselves to spiritual abundance. It is convenient to take these holy souls not only men, but also angels, if we want to understand here that all things are subject to our Lord Jesus Christ. Because there is no creature that is not submitted to what the primates of the spirit submit, so to speak. But how do we prove that the sheep can be taken in a sublime sense not only by men, but also by the blessed spirits of the angelic creature? Is it because of what the Lord says that he abandoned ninety-nine sheep on the mountain, that is, in the highest places, and that he came down because of one? If we take for the one lost sheep all the souls that fell in Adam, since Eve was made from his side, and of which there is now no time to speak and consider them spiritually, all that remains is for us to understand that the ninety-nine left on the mountains are not human spirits, but angelic ones. 1 [v. l j. This psalm is titled: To the end, through the arcana of the Son. Psalm of David. One can inquire into the arcana of the Son; but since he did not add whose son he was, it should be understood that he speaks of the only begotten Son of God. For when it comes to the son of David, the psalm is intitviia: When he fled from the presence of Absalom, his son. Having mentioned the name of the son, and, therefore, not being able to hide who was being spoken of, however, it was not only said about the presence of Absalom the younger, but his own was added. Here, by not adding "his" son and, adeligi et explicari possunt, sed pro locis; namque alibi aliud significant. Et haec regula in omni allegoria retinenda est, ut pro sententia praesentis loci considertur quod per similarityinem dicitur; haec est enim dominica et apostolica discipline. Repetamus ergo ultimum versum qui etiam in principle Psalmi ponitur, et laudemus Deum dicentes: Domine Dominas noster, quam admirable est nonien tuum in universa terral Decenter quippe post textum sermonis ad caput teditur, quo totus idem sermo referendus est. PSALMUS

1 [v.l}. Psalmi huius incriptio est: In finem pro occultis Filii, Psttlmus ipsi David. De occultis Filii quaeri potest: sed quia non addidit cuius, ipsum unigenitum Dei Filium oportet intelligi. Ubi enim de filio David Psalmus inscriptus est, Cum fugeret, inquit, a facie Abessalon filii sui (Ps 3,1); cum et nomen eius dictum esset, et ob hoc latere non posset de quo diceretur, non tamen dictum est tantum, a facie Abessalon filii, sed additum est, sui. Hic vero, et quod non additum est, sui, et quod de Gentibus plana dicit, non potest recte accipi Abessalon: ñeque enim bellum quod cum patre ille perditus gessit, ullo moda ad Gentes

moreover, speaking many things about the Gentiles, the son cannot be rightly taken for Absalom; Likewise, the war that that ill-fated son unleashed against his father does not refer in any way to the Gentiles, when there only the people of Israel are divided against themselves. Therefore, this psalm is sung because of the arcana of the only begotten Son of God; because the Lord himself, when without addition he names the Son where he says: If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free, he wants Him to be understood as the Only Begotten of God. It certainly does not say, Son of God; but, nevertheless, by saying only Son, he implies whose Son he is. This locution is only tolerated by the excellence of Him of whom we speak, in such a way that, although we do not mention Him, it can be understood to whom it refers; Thus we say it rains, it calms, it thunders and other similar things, and we do not add who does it, because, without thinking about it, the excellence of the executor is presented to the mind and, therefore, does not need an explanatory word. What are the arcana of the Son? First of all, it must be understood that in this word, arcane, some manifest things of the Son are contained, from which those that are called hidden are distinguished. Therefore, since we believe in two comings of the Lord: in a past one, which the Jews did not notice, and in another future one, which both of us await, and since this one, which the Jews did not understand, benefited the Gentiles, it is conveniently understood to have been said in it because of the arcana of the Son, in which the obstinacy on the part of Israel was carried out so that the fullness of the Gentiles could enter. If anyone reconsiders, they will observe that two judgments are also hinted at in Scripture: one hidden, the other mapertinet, cum populus tantum Israel adversus se ibi divisus sit. Canitur ¡taque iste psalmus pro occultis unigeniti Filii Dei. Nam et ipse Dominus cum sine additamento ponit Filium, seipsum unigenitum vult intelligi ubi ait: Si vos Filias liberaverit, tune veré liberi eritis (lo 8,36). Non enim dixit, Filius Dei; sed tantum saying Filias, dat intelligi cuius sit filius. Quam locutionem non recipit nisi excellentia eius de quo ita loquimur, ut etíamsi non eurn nominemus, possit intelligi: ita enim dicimus, Pluit, serenat, tonat, et si qua sunt talia, nec addimus quis id faciat; quia omnium mentibus sponte sese offert excellentia facientis, nec verba desiderat. Quae sunt igitur oeculta Filii?

In quo verbo primum intelligendum est esse aliqua Filii manifesta, a quibus distinguuntur haec quae appellantur oeculta. Quamobrem, quoniam duos adventus Domini credimus, unum praeteritum, quem Iudaei non intellexerunt, alterum futurum, quem utrique speramus; et quoniam iste quem Iudaei non intellexerunt, Gentibus profuit, non inconvenient accipitur de hoc adventu dici, pro occultis Filii, ubi caecitas ex parte Israel facta est, ut plenitudo Gentium intraret (Rom 11,25). Duo etiam iudicia insinuantur per Scripturas, si quis adveitat; unum occultum, alterum manifestum. Occultum nunc agitur, de quo apostolus Petrus dicit: Tempus est ut iudiíiitm incipiat a domo Donini (1 Petr 4,17). Occultum ¡taque iudi-

nifesto. The hidden one is taking place now, and the apostle Saint Peter says of it: It is time for the judgment to begin at the house of the Lord. The hidden judgment is the punishment by which each man is now either tormented to purify himself, or is warned to convert, or, if he despises the calling and teaching of God, is blinded to condemn himself. The manifest judgment, to which the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead, is confessed by all to be that in which the good will be rewarded and the evil will be punished. But then that confession will not serve as a remedy for evils, but rather as the height of condemnation. Regarding these two judgments: one hidden, the other open, it seems to me that the Lord spoke when he said: Whoever believes in me passes from death to life and will not come to judgment, that is, to open judgment. The passage from death to life with few anguish and afflictions with which he punishes everyone he receives as a son, is the hidden judgment. He who does not believe, he says, is already judged; That is to say, whoever does not believe in the current hidden judgment is already prepared for that other patent one. We also find these two judgments in the Book of Wisdom, where we read: For this reason, as you gave judgment to children without sense to ridicule, and those who were not corrected by this judgment, would suffer? the worthy judgment of God. Those who do not correct themselves with this hidden judgment of God will justly be punished with the manifest one. Therefore, in this psalm the hidden things of the Son must be noted, that is, his humble coming, with which he profited the Gentiles and blinded the Jews, and the punishment that is now secretly carried out, but not yet for the condemnation of sinners, but for the exercise of concium est poena, qua nunc unusquisque hominum aut exercetur ad purgationem, aut admonetur ad conversionem, aut si contempserit vocationem et disciplinan! Dei, excaecatur ad damnationem. Iudicium autem manifestum est, quo venturus Dominus iudicabit vivos et mortuos, omnibus fatentibus eurn esse a quo et bonis praemia, et malis supplicia tribuentur. Sed tune illa confessio, non ad remedium malorum, sed ad cumulum damnationis valebit.

De his duobus iudiciis, uno oceulto, alio manifesto, videtur mihi Dominus dixisse, ubi ait: Qui in me credit, transit de morle ad vitam, nec in iudicium veniet (lo 5,24), in iudicium scilicet manifestum: nam hoc quod transit de morle ad vitam per nonnullam afflictionem, qua fiagellat omnem filium quem recipit, iudicium oceultum est; Qui autem non credit, inquit, iam iudicatus est (Ib. 3,18); id est, isto oceulto iudicio iam praeparatus est ad illud manifestum. Haec duo iudicia etiam in Sapientia legimus, ubi scriptum est: Propter hoc tanquam pueris insensatis iudicium in derisum dedisti; hi autem hoc iudicio non correcti, dignum Dei iudicium experti sunt (Wis 12,25-26). Qui ergo non corriguntur isto oceulto Dei iudicio, dignissime illo manifested punishment. Quocirca in hoc psalmo observanda sunt oceulta Filii, id est, et humilis eius adventus quo profuit Gentibus cum caecitate Iudaeorum, et poena quae never oceulte agitur, nondum damnatione pec-

pourings, or for a warning of conversion, or for blindness, so that those who do not want to convert may prepare for punishment. 2 [v. 2]. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart. He does not confess God with all his heart who doubts something of His providence, but who already sees the hidden things of the Wisdom of God and who notices how great the invisible reward is, which goes so far as to say: We glory in tribulations, and who also understands how all the torments that are inflicted bodily serve either to exercise those converted to God, or to warn them to convert, or, finally, to prepare for the just condemnation the hardened of heart, and thus in this way all things that fools judge to be carried out by chance and inconsiderately and without divine administration are referred to the government of divine providence. I will tell all your wonders. He tells of all the wonders of God who notes that they are performed not only visibly in bodies, but invisibly in souls, although in a much more sublime and excellent way. Because earthly men given to hidden things are more amazed at the resurrection of the dead body of Lazarus than at the resurrection of the soul of Paul the persecutor. But, as the visible miracle calls or leads the soul to admiration, the invisible one illuminates the one who, called, came. He narrates all the wonders of God who, believing the visible things, passes to the understanding of the invisible. 3 {[v.3j. I will rejoice and rejoice in you. No longer in this world, not in the pleasure of bodily contact, nor in the flavors of the palacantium, sed aut exercitatione conversorum, aut admonitione ut convertantur, aut caecitate ut damnationi praeparentur qui convertedí noluerint. 2 fv.2]. Conjilebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo. Non in toto corde confitetur Deo, qui de providentia eius in aliquo dubitat: sed qui iam cernit oceulta sapientiae Dei, quantum sit invisibile praemium eius, qui dicit, Gaudemus in tribuUtionibus (Rom 5,3); et quemadmodum omnes cruciatus, qui corporaliter inferuntur aut exerceant conversos ad Deum, aut ut convertantur admoneant, aut iustae damnationi ultime praeparent obduratos, et sic omnia ad dii'inae providentiae regime referantur, quae stulti quasi casu et fearé et nulla divina administratione fieri putant. I narrate omnia mirabilia tita.

Narrat omnia mirabilia Dei, qui ea non solum in corporibus palam, sed in animis invisibiliter quidem, sed longe sublimius et excellentius fieri videt. Nam terreni homines et oceultis dediti, magis mirantur resurrexisse in corpore mortuum Lazarum, quam resurrexisse in anima persecutorem Paulum. Sed quoniam visible miraculum ad illuminationem animam vocat, invisibile autem eam quae vocata venit illuminat; omnia narrat mirabilia Dei, qui credens visibilibus ad intelligenda invisibüia transitum facit. 3 [v.3]. Laetabor, et exsdtabo in te. Non iam in hoc saeculo; non in voluptate contrectationis corporum, nec in palati et linguae saporibus,

give and language, nor in the perfume of odors, nor in the delight of the sounds that pass, nor in the shapes of bodies tinged with various colors, nor in the vanity of human praise, nor in marriage and offspring that must die, nor in superfluous earthly riches, nor in the investigation of this world, or of the things that extend through spaces or unfold with the succession of times, but I I will rejoice and rejoice in you, namely, in the hidden things of the Son, where the light of your face is impressed on us, O Lord, because it says: You will hide them in the hidden part of your face. He who narrates all your wonders will be glad and rejoice in you. Since it has now been spoken prophetically, he who did not come to do his will, but the will of the one who sent him, will narrate all your wonders. 4 [v. 4]. The person of the Lord is already beginning to appear speaking in this psalm, as it continues in this way: I will sing to your name, O Most High!, turning back my enemy. When did this enemy retreat? Was it when he was told: Satan, turn back? Then the one who tempted wanted to prevail, retreated, neither deceiving the tempted nor prevailing over him. The earthly men are placed behind; the celestial man was made first, despite appearing second; The first man, coming from the earth, was earthly; the second, from the sky, celestial; but he was of the same stock as him by whom it was said, He that cometh after me was made greater than I. The Apostle forgets the things that are behind and reaches out to those ahead. The enemy turned back, sive quae successione temporis volvitur: sed laetabor et exsultabo in te, videlicet in occultis Filü, ubi signatum est in nobis lumen vultus tui, Domine (Ps 4,7); etenim Abscondes eos, inquit, in abscondito vultus tui (Ps 30,21). Laetabitur ergo et exsultabit in te, qui narrat omnia mirabilia tua.

Narrabit autem omnia mirabilia tua, siquidem nunc per prophetiam dictum est, ule qui non venit voluntatem suam faceré, sed voluntatem eius qui eum misit (lo 6,38). 4 [v.4], Iam enim incipit apparere persona Domini in hoc psalmo loquens. Nam sequitur: Psallam nomini tuo, Altissime, in convertendo inimicum meutn retrorsum. Huius ergo inimicus when retro conversus is? Even when the dictum is: Redi retro, Satan? (Mt 4,10); tune enim qui tentando se praeponere cupiebat retro factus est, non decipiendo tentatum et in eum nihil valendo. Retro enim sunt terreni nomines; caelestis autem homo prior factus est quamvis post venerit: primus enim homo de terra terrenus; secundus homo de cáelo caelestis (1 Cor 15:47). Sed de ipsa stirpe veniebat, a quo dictum est: Qui post me venit, ante me factus est (lo 1,15). Et Apostolus ea quae retro sunt obliviscitur, et in ea quae

He was able to deceive the celestial man when he was tempted, and he went to the lands where he can dominate. Therefore, no man precedes and puts to flight the enemy, except he who, laying down the image of the earthly man, bears the image of the celestial. If, on the other hand, we prefer to take what was said: my enemy, in a universal sense, for the sinful man or the Gentile, will not be an absurdity; nor will what was written be a punishment: turning my enemy back, but a benefit; and such a benefit that no other can be compared to this. What is happier than to abandon pride and not want to precede Christ, as if he were healthy and did not need a doctor, but rather preferring to follow Christ, who, calling the disciple to perfect him, says to him: Follow me? However, it is more appropriately understood to have been said of the devil turning my enemy back. For the devil, without a doubt, is also driven back in the persecution of the righteous, and is much more useful in persecution than if he preceded as prince and leader. It must be sung to the name of the Most High, turning the enemy back, because we must prefer to flee in pursuit. He must continue to guide us, since we have somewhere to flee and hide: in the hidden things of the Son, since the Lord became our refuge. 5 [v. 51. They will weaken and perish before your face. Who will weaken and perish but the wicked and wicked? They will weaken, having no power, and they will perish, because they will cease to be impious before the presence of God, that is, by knowing God, ante sunt extendit (Phil 3:13). Conversus est igitur inimicus retro, postquam non valuit hominem caelestem decipere tentatum, et se ad terrains convertit ubi dominari potest. Quapropter nullus hominum eum praecedit et retro eum esse facit, nisi qui deponens imaginem terreni hominis portaverit imaginem caelestis (1 Cor 15:49). Iam vero si quod dictum est, inimicum meum, generaliter vel peccatorem vel gentilem hominem magis velimus accipere, non erit absurdum. Nec poena erit quod dictum est, In covertendo inimicum meum retrorsum; sed beneficium, et tale beneficium, ut huic compare nihil possit.

Quid enim beatius quam deponere superbiam, et non velle Christum praecedere, veluti sanus sit cui medicus non sit necessarius; sed malle retro iré post Christum, qui discipulum vocans ut perficiatur, dicit: Sequere me? (Mt 19,21). Sed tamen accommodatius de diabolo dictum intelligitur: In convertendo inimicum meum retrorsum. Diabolus quippe retrorsum conversus est etiam in persecutione iustorum, et multo utilius persecutor est, quam si dux et princeps praeiret. Psallendum est igitur nomini Altissími in convertendo inimicum retrorsum; quoniam malle debenmus eum persequentem fugere, quam ducentem sequi: habemus enim quo fugiamus et abscondamur in occultis Filü, quia Dominus factus est refugium nobis (Ps 89,1). 5 [v.5]. Injirmabuntur, et peribunt a facie tua. Qui infirmabuntur et peribunt, nisi iniqui et impii? Injirmabuntur, dum nihil valebunt; et peribunt, quia non erunt impii; a facie Dei, id est a cognitione Dei, sicut

for they will perish as he perished who said, I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Why will the wicked weaken and perish before your presence? Because, he says, you made the judgment and the cause mine, that is, you made me or that judgment in which I seemed to be judged, and you made me the cause in which, being just and innocent, men condemned me. These things were at his side in the fight for our liberation. In the same way, sailors call their own the wind that they take advantage of to sail prosperously. 6. You sat on the throne, you who judge equity. Whether the Son says this to the Father; because he said: You would not have power in me if it had not been given to you from above, referring it to the equity of the Father and the arcana of the Son, since the judge of men was judged for the benefit of men, or whether the man said to God: you seated him on the throne, you who judge equity, calling his soul a throne, perhaps his body being the earth, which was called his footstool, since God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, or whether the soul also said to her husband of the perfect Church, without spot or blemish, that is, worthy of knowing the hidden things of the Son, because the king brought her into his chamber: You sat on the throne, you who judge equity, because you rose from the dead and ascended to heaven and are seated at the right hand of the Father; In this case, any of these sentences that are chosen in order to make this verse known, none of them surpass the rule of faith. periit ille qui dixit: Vivo autem iam non ego, vivit autem in me Christus (Gal 2,20). Sed quare infirmabuntur, et peribunt impii a facie tita? Quoniam jecisti iudicium meum, inquit, et causam meam: id est, iudicium illud in quo iudicari visus sum, meum fecisti; et causam illam in qua me iustum et innocentem homines damnaverunt, meam fecisti. Haec enim ei militaverunt ad nostram liberationem: sicut et nautae dicunt ventum suum, quo utuntur ad bene navigandum. 6. Sedisti super thronum, qui indicas aequitatem.

Sive Filius Patri dicat, qui etiam illud dixit, Non haberes in me potestatetn, nisi tibi datum juisset desuper (lo 19,11), idipsum ad aequitatem Patris et ad occulta sua referens, quod iudex hominum ad utilitatem hominem iudicatus est: sive homo dicat Deo, Sedisti super thronum, qui indicas aequitatem, animam suam thronum eius appellans, ut corpus sit fortasse terra, quae scabellum pedum eius dicta est (Is 66,1); Deus enim erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi (2 Cor 5,19): sive anima Ecclesiae iam perfection et sine macula et ruga (Eph 5,27), dignified scilicet occultis Filii, quia introduxit eam rex in cubiculum suum (Cant 1,3), dicat sponso suo, Sedisti super thronum, qui indicas aequitatem, quia resurrexisti a mortuis, et ascendisti in caelum, et sedes ad dexteram Patris: quaelibet ergo harum sententia placeat, quo iste versus referatur, regulam fidei non excedit.

7 [v. 6]. You rebuked the people and the wicked perished. We understand more exactly that this was said of our Lord Jesus Christ than that He said it. Who else rebuked the nations and the wicked perished but the one who, after ascending to heaven, sent the Holy Spirit, with whom the apostles were filled, boldly preached the word of God and argued with complete freedom from sin to men, with whose rebuke the wicked perished, because the wicked was justified and became pious? You blotted out his name in the century, and in the century of the century. The name of the wicked was erased, because those who already believe in God are not called wicked. His name is erased in the century, that is, while the temporal century unfolds. And it is also erased in the century of the century. What is the century of the century but a reality of which this century is the image and shadow? The change of times, which follow one another, when the moon diminishes and becomes full again, when the sun returns to its place after a full year, when spring, or summer, or autumn, or winter so pass that they return, is a certain imitation of eternity. But the century of this century is what constitutes immutable eternity. As the verse is found in the soul and also in the voice, and the former is understood and the latter is heard, and the former modifies the latter, and, therefore, the former works in art and remains and the latter sounds in the air and passes away, so the changeable measure of this century is determined or limited by the immutable century, which is called the century of the century. That is why the former remains in the Art of God, that is, in Wisdom and Virtue; but this develops in the administration or government 7 [v.6]. Increpasti gentes, et periit impius. Convenientius hoc Domino Iesu Christo dici, quam ipsum dicere, accipimus. Quis enim alius increpavit gentes, et periit impius, nisi qui postea quam ascendit in caelum, misit Spiritum sanctum, quo completi Apostoli, cum fiducia praedicarent verbum Dei, et peccata hominum libere arguerent? qua increpatione periit impius; quia iustificatus est impius, et factus est pius. Nornen eorum delesli in saeculum, et saeculum saeculi. Deletum est nomen impiorum: non enim appellantur impii, qui Deo vero credunt. Deletur autem nomen eorum in saeculum, id est, quamdiu temporale saeculum volvitur.

Et iu saeculum saeculi. Quid est saeculum saeculi, nisi cuius effigiem et tanquam umbram habet hoc saeculum? Vicissitudo enim temporum sibi succedentium, dum luna minuitur et rursus impletur, dum sol omni anno locum suum repetit, dum ver, vel aestas, vel autumnus, vel hiems sic transit ut redeat, aeternitatis quaedam imitatio est. Sed huius saeculi saeculum est quod incommutabili aeternitate consistit. Sicut versus in animo, et versus in voce: ille intelligitur, iste auditur; et ille istum modification: et ideo ille in arte operatur et manet, iste in aere sonat et transit. Sic huius mutabilis saeculi modus ab illo incommutabili saeculo definitur, quod dícitur saeculum saeculi: et ideo illud in arte Dei, hoc est in Sapientia et Virtute permanet; hoc autem in creaturae administratione peragitur. Si tamen non repetitio est, ut postea quam dictum est in saeculum, ne hoc

of the creature. However, if the word in saeculum is not a repetition, so that the word in saeculum that was recorded again would not be understood as something that happens, in saeculum saeculi was added. In the Greek copies it is written like this: £ts TÓV CXÍWVOC, KCCÍ eis TÓV cxicovcc TOÜ ccicovos, which many Latins translated not in saeculum, et in saeculum saeculi (in the century and in the century of the century), but in aeternum, et in saeculum saeculi (eternally and for ever and ever); so that in what was said in saeculum saeculi the same thing that was said in aeternum could be understood. Then you blotted out the name of the wicked forever, for from now on there will never be any wicked. If his name does not increase in this century, much less in the century of the century. 8 [v. 7]. The swords of the enemy failed forever. The word inimici (enemies) should not be taken in the plural, but in the genitive singular (of the enemy). Of what enemy did the swords fail but of the devil? By swords are understood the various propositions of error, with which the devil kills souls as with swords. To defeat these swords and render them useless is the sword of which it was said in Psalm 7: If you do not convert, he will brandish his sword; and perhaps this is the end to which the enemy's swords will come to pass, because even they retain a certain value. She works now hiddenly; In the last judgment he will act uncovered. With this he will destroy the cities, since he goes on to say: The swords of the enemy have failed forever, and you have destroyed the cities, the cities in which the devil reigns, where the deceitful and fraudulent councils reside as a senate, to whose principality acomacciperetur quod transit, subiieeretur in saeculum saeculi. Nam in graecis exemplaribus sic est: gis TÓV ccicovcc, Kai sis TÓV ccicovcc TOÜ aicovos; quod Latiní plerique interpretati sunt, non in saeculum, et in saeculum saeculi, sed in aeternum, et in saeculum saeculi: ut in eo quod dictum est in saeculum saeculi, illud exposeretur quod dictum est in aeternum. Nomen ergo impiorum delesli in aeternum, quia deinceps nunquam erunt impii. Et si in hoc saeculum non tenditur nomen eorum, multo minus in saeculum saeculi. 8 [v.7]. Inimici décerunt jrameae in jinem. Non pluraliter inimici, sed singulariter huius inimici. Cuius autem inimici, nisi diaboli frameae defecerunt?

Hae autem intelliguntur diverse opinions erroris, quibus ille animas tanquam gladiis perirm't. His gladiis vincendis et ad defectum perducendis instat ille gladius, de quo in seventh psalmo dicitur: Nisi con-' vertamini, gladiutn suum vihrabit (Ps 7,13). Et forte iste est finís in quem frameae deficiunt inimici, quia usque ad ipsum aliquid valent; ipse nunc operatur oceulte, ultimo autem judicio palam vibrabitur. Hoc destruuntur civitates; nam ita sequitur, Inimici dejacerunt jrameae in jinem; et civitates destruxisti: civitates autem in quibus diabolus regnat, ubi dolosa et fraudulenta consilia tanquam curiae locum obtinent, cui principatui quasi satellites et ministri adsunt officia quorumque membrorum, oculi ad cu-

They serve as escorts and ministers the services or jobs of each of the members: the eyes for curiosity, the ears for lasciviousness or, if there is something that is gladly heard in a bad sense, the hands for plunder or for any other crime or evil, and the other members who assist the tyrannical prince in this measure, that is, who militate under his perverse advice. The lower town of this city is made up of all the licentious affections and turbulent movements of the spirit that promote daily seditions in man. Therefore, where there is a king, senate, ministers and people, there is a city; But such components would not exist in bad cities if they were not first found in each man, which are like the elements and seeds of cities. Destroy these cities when the prince has been cast out from there, of whom it was said: The prince of this world has been cast out; With the word of truth these kingdoms are annihilated, evil counsels are killed, clumsy affections are tamed, the offices of the members and senses are paralyzed and they are assigned to the militia of justice and good works, so that, as the Apostle says, sin does not reign in our mortal body and the other things that he says in this place. Then the soul is pacified and man sets out to conquer rest and bliss. His memory perished with an uproar, that is, the wicked perished. But it was said with noise or uproar, either because noise is made when impiety is destroyed, since it does not pass to the utmost peace, where the deepest silence exists, unless it is the one who has first fought with great noise against its vices, or so that the memory of the impious perishes, it disappears.

riositatem, aures ad lasciviam, vel si quid est aliud quod in malam partem libenter auditur, manus ad rapiñara vel quodlibet aliud facinus aut flagitium, et membra caetera in hunc modum tyrannico principatui, id est perversis consiliis militantia. Huius civitatis quasi plebs est omnes delicatae affectiones et turbulenti motus animi, quotidianas seditiones in homine agitantes. Ergo ubi rex, ubi curia, ubi ministri, ubi plebs invenitur, civitas est; ñeque enim talia essent in malis civitatibus, nisi prius essent in singulis hominibus, qui sunt tanquam elementa et semina civitatum. Has civitates destruit, cum excluso inde principe, de quo dictum est, Princeps huius saeculi missus est joras (lo 12,31), vastantur haec regna verbo veritatis, sopiuntur maligna consilia, turpes affectiones edomantur, membrorum et sensuum ministeria captivantur, et ad iustitiae et bonorum operum militiam transíeruntur: ut iam, sicut Apostolus dicit, non regnet peccatum in nostro mortdi corpore (Rom 6,12), et caetera huius loci. Tune pacatur anima, et ordinatur homo ad quietem et ad beatitudem capessendam. Periit memoria eorum cum strepitu: impiorum scilicet. Sed cum strepitu, sive quia fit strepitus, dictum est, cum impietas evertitur; non enim transit ad summam pacem, ubi summum silentium est, nisi qui magno strepitu prius cum suis vitiis belligeraverit: sive cum stre-

also making the same noise, with which impiety stirs up. 9 [v.8.9]. And the Lord remains eternally. Why did the heathen roar and the people meditate vain things against the Lord and against his Christ, when the Lord remains eternally? He prepared His seat in judgment, and He Himself will judge the world of the earth in equity. He prepared his seat when he was judged, for man obtained heaven through that patience, and God took advantage of those who believed in Man, and this is the hidden judgment of the Son. But since he must also come clearly and clearly to judge the living and the dead, he prepared his seat in the hidden judgment, and the same, equally revealed, will judge the globe of the earth in equity; That is to say, taking into account the merits of each one, he will distribute what he deserves, placing the lambs on the right and the goats on the left. He will judge the people with justice. This is what was said before: he will judge the world of the earth in equity, not as men judge, who do not see the hearts, by whom the worst are most often acquitted rather than condemned; but the Lord will judge equitably and justly, the conscience bearing witness and the thought accusing or defending. 10 [v.10]. And the Lord gives you refuge for the poor. No matter how much the enemy who turned back pursues, with what will he harm those for whom the Lord made himself a refuge? This will happen if in this world, of which he is magistrate, men pitu dictum est, ut pereat memoria impiorum etiam ipso strepitu pereunte, in quo tumultuatur ímpietas. 9 [v.8.9]. Et Dominas in aetemum permanet. Utquid ergo fremuerunt gentes, et populi meditan' sunt inania, adversus Dominum et adversus Christum eius? (Ps 2,1); nam Dominas in aetemum permanet. Paravit, cum iudicatus est, sedem suam: per íllam enim patientiam homo caelum acquisivit, et Deus in nomine credentibus profuit; et hoc est occultum Filii iudicium. Sed quia etiam palam manifesteque venturus est ad vivos et mortuos iudicandos, paravit in occulto iudicio sedem suam; et ipse Item palam iudicabit orbem terrarum in aequitate, id est meritis dignified distribuet, agnos ad dexteramponers, haedos ad sinistram (Mt 25,33). Judicabit populos cum iustitia.

Hoc est quod superius dictum est, Iudicabit orbem terrarum in aequitate: non quemadmodum iudicant nomines, qui corda non vident, a quibus plerumque deteriores absolvuntur quam condemnantur; thirst in aequitate et cum iustitia Dominus judicabit, testimonium perhibente conscientia, et cogitationibus accusantibus seu defenderntibus (Rom 2,15). 10 [v.10]. Et jactus est Dominus refugium pauperi. Quantumlibet persequatur inimicus ille, qui conversus est retro, quid nocebit eís quorum refugium factus est Dominus? Sed hoc fiet, si in saeculo hoc, cuius

They chose to be poor, not loving anything that either living or loving here he would have abandoned, or what is abandoned for someone who dies; For such a poor person the Lord became a refuge, a helper in opportunities, in tribulation. In this way he makes poor, because he scourges everyone whom he accepts as a son. How helpful he is in opportunities or in situations, he declared when he added in the tribulation, because the soul does not return to God except when it departs from this world, and it does not depart from the world on a better occasion than when pains and labors are mixed with its lies and evil and pernicious pleasures. 11 [v. l l ]. And let those who know your name hope in you: when they had stopped hoping for riches and other flattery of this world. The knowledge of the name of God opportunely receives the soul that seeks where to fix its hope when it has been separated from this world. Indeed, the very name of God was now spread throughout the world; But knowledge of the name is achieved when the one who bears the name is known, since the name is not a name simply because it is a name, but because of what it means or represents. It was said his name is, Lord. Therefore, whoever submits himself to God willingly as a servant knows this name. And let those who know your name wait for you. The Lord also said to Moses: I am who I am, and you will say to the children of Israel: He who is sent me. Then let those who know your name hope in you, so that they do not put their hope in these things that slide with the change of time, having nothing more than the will be and the was, because lo ille magistratus est, pauperes esse delegerint, nihil amarndo quod vel hic vivostem aut amorem deserit, vel a moriente deseritur; tali enim pauperi refugium factus est Dominus, Adiutor in opportunitatibus, in tribulatione. Sic pauperes facit, quoniam flagellat omnem filium quem recipit (Hebr 12:6). Nam quid sit adiutor in opportunitatibus, exposuit cum addidit, in tribulatione: non enim convertitur anima ad Deum, nisi dum ab hoc saeculo avertitur; nec opportunius ab hoc saeculo avertitur, nisi nugatoriis eius et noxiis et pernicosis voluptatibus labores dolorsque misceantur. 11 [v. l l ]. Et sperent in te qui cognoscunt nomen tuum: cum destiterint sperare in divitiis et in alus huius saeculi blandimentis.

Quaerentem quippe animam ubi figat spem, cum ab hoc mundo avellitur, opportune excipit cognitio nominis Dei: nam nomen ipsum Dei nunc usquequaque vulgatum est; sed cognitio nominis est, cum ille cognoscitur cuius est nomen: non enim nomen propter se nomen est, sed propter id quod significat. Dictum est autem, Dominus nomen est Mi (Jer 33,2). Quapropter qui se libenter Deo farnulum subdit, cognovit hoc nomen. Et sperent in te qui cognoscunt nomen tuum. item Dominus dicit ad Moysen: Ego sum qui sum; et dices filiis Israel: Misit me qui est (Ex 3,14). Sperent ergo in te qui cognoscunt nomen tuum: ne sperent in his rebus quae temporis volubilitate praeterfluunt, nihil habentes nisi, erit, et Fuit; quoniam quod in illis futurum est, cum venerit, fit statim praeteritum; exspectatur

that in them it is future, when it has arrived, it instantly becomes past; The future is eagerly awaited and lost with pain. In the nature of God there will be nothing, as if it is not yet, nor was there anything, as if it is no longer, but it is as much as it is, and it is eternity. Those who know the name of Him who said: I am who I am, and of whom it was said: He who is sent me, stop hoping and loving temporal things and turn to eternal hope. Because you did not abandon those who seek you. Those who seek him no longer seek fleeting and perishable things, since no one can serve two masters. £12 v. l 2 }. Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion. This is said to those who the Lord does not abandon when seeking Him. He himself dwells in Zion, which means observation and is an image of the current Church, as Jerusalem is of the future Church, that is, of the city of the saints, who already enjoy the angelic life, since Jerusalem means a vision of peace. Observation precedes vision, as the current Church precedes the immortal and eternal city that is promised. It precedes in time, not in dignity, because where we aspire to reach is more honorable than what we execute so that we deserve to arrive, and to achieve the vision we put observation into practice. The most diligent observation would fall into error if God did not dwell in the same Church that now exists in the world. To this Church it was said: The temple of God is holy, which is you; and also: Christ dwells within man through the faith in your hearts. Then we are commanded to sing to the Lord who dwells cum cupiditate, amittitur cum dolore. In Dei autem natura non erit aliquid, quasi nondum sit; aut Fuit, quasi iam non sit: sed est tantum id quod est, et ipsa est aeternitas. Desinant igitur sperare et diligere temporalia, et se »d aeternam spem conferant, qui cognoscunt nomen eius qui dixit: Ego stim qui sum, et de quo dictum est: Misit me qui est. Quoniam non dereliquisti quaerentes te, Domine. Qui eum quaerunt, iam transeuntia et moritura non quaerunt: nemo enim potest duobus dominis I will serve (Mt 6:24). 12 [v.12]. Psallite Domino, qui habitat in Sion: his dicitur, quos non derelinquit quaerentes se Dominus.

Ipse habitat in Zion, quod interpretatur Speculatio, et gestat imaginem Ecclesiae quae mine est: sicut Ierusalem gestat imaginem Ecclesiae quaefutura est, id est civitatis sanctorum iam angelica vita fruentium; quia Ierusalem interpretatur Visio pacis. Praecedit autem speculatio visionem, sicut ista Ecclesia praecedit eam quae promittitur, civitatem immortalem et aeternam. Sed praecedit tempore, non dignitate: quia honorabilius est quo pervenire mtimur, quam id quod agimus, ut pervenire mereamur; agimus autem speculationem, ut perveniamus ad visionem. Sed etiam ipsam, quae nunc est, Ecclesiam nisi Dominus inhabitaret, iret in errorem quamlibet studiosissima speculatio: et huic Ecclesiae dictum est, Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod eslis vos (1 Cor 3,17); et, In interiore homine habitare Christum per fidem in cordibus vestris (Eph 3,16). Praecipitur ergo nobis ut psallamus Domino, qui

in Zion, that we may praise with one accord the Lord who dwells in the Church. Announce among the people its wonders: it was done and it does not stop being done. 13 [v. 13]. Because he agreed to demand their blood. This is said as if those who were sent to evangelize were responding to the command that was ordered: Announce among the nations his wonders, and saying: Lord, who believed what he heard from us? And for your sake we are wounded throughout the day, conveniently continuing by saying that the Christians who will die in persecution will not die without great fruit of eternity, because it was remembered by demanding their blood. Why did you prefer to say their blood? Perhaps as if some ignorant person with diminished faith asked saying: How will they announce, since the infidelity of the people was going to be cruel to them, and the answer was: Because it was agreed upon by demanding their blood, that is, the last judgment will come, where the glory of the murdered and the punishment of the murderers will be manifested? Let no one think that it was written and remembered as if there were room for forgetting in God. It was noted this way because after a long time the judgment must take place, and, therefore, attention was paid to the disposition of weak men, who consider God forgetful because He does not act as soon as they want. The following is also said to these: He did not forget the cry of the poor. That is to say, it was not forgotten as you think. This is as if, after they heard it was remembered, they said: Then there was habitation in Sion, ut concorditer Dominum Ecclesiae inhabitatorem laudemus. Annuniiítte Inter gentes mirabilia eius: et factum est, et non desinet fieri. 13 [v. l 3 j. Quoniam requirens sanguinem eorum memoratus est. Quasi responderetur ab his qui missi sunt evangelizare, illi praecepto quod dictum est, Annuntiale Inter gentes mitabilia eius; et diceretur, Domine, quis credidit auditui nostro? (Is 53,1) et, Propter te occidimur tota die (Ps 43,22), convenientr sequitur, dicens, non sine magno fructu aeternitatis morituros in persecutione Christianos: Quoniam requirens sanguinem eorum memoratus est. Sed cur sanguinem eorum maluit dicere?

An quasi alius imperitior et minoris fidei quaereret dices, Quomodo annuntiabunt, cum in eos infidelitas gentium saevitura sit; huic respondertur, Quoniam requirens sanguinem eorum memoratus est; Id est, veniet ultimum iudicium, ubi et interfectorum gloria, et interficientium poena manifesta sit? Memoratus est autem, nemo ita positum putet, quasi oblivio cadat in Deum; sed quia post longum tempus futurum est iudicium, secundum affectum infirmorum hominum positum est, qui quasi oblitum Deum putant, quia non tam cyto facit quam ipsi volunt. His dicitur etiam quod sequitur, Non est oblitus clamorem pauperum; id est, non ut putatis obli-
